rules.note: Distilled from the eleven references above. This genre's construction is NOT the simulator's: where the simulator identifies itself with a thick near-black stroke, an overhanging plaque and a red circle hanging off the corner, the neutral theme identifies itself with proportional sizing, translucency, generous padding and a pixel ceiling on every touch target. Numbers below are the ones the sources state; where a value is a range, the sources disagree only in degree and the range is the honest reading.

sizingUnits.rule: author Size and Position in SCALE; use offset only where the engine allows nothing else (UIStroke.Thickness, UIPadding, small nudges like a 10px corner inset)
sizingUnits.clampWith: UISizeConstraint for pixel floors and ceilings, UIAspectRatioConstraint for anything that must stay square
sizingUnits.workedConversion: 100x100 pixels ~= 0.257 scale on both axes at the reference viewport
sizingUnits.why: the staff post gives the conversion and the curriculum sizes every HUD part as a percentage of the screen; a neutral UI is judged on whether it survives a phone and a 21:9 monitor, and fixed pixel rectangles are the thing that fails that test first

cornerRadius.why: the staff post states an offset radius 'appears drastically different between devices' and the reference docs explain that scale measures against the shortest edge, so 0.5 is reliably a pill and a chosen scale keeps the same visual softness on every screen — this single habit is the clearest tell of platform-native construction

targetSize.howToApply: size in scale, then cap with UISizeConstraint MaxSize (inf, 44); treat 44 as the floor on touch as well
targetSize.why: Roblox's shipped experience controls are 44px and the announcement says that number was chosen to hit WCAG 2.1 target size at AAA, and Roblox's own settings-menu tutorial independently caps its opener at MaxSize (inf, 44) — two separate Roblox sources landing on the same number makes it a platform convention rather than a preference

panelSurface.rule: the panel floats over the running world and lets it show through; it is not an opaque sheet and it does not tile a texture
panelSurface.why: the settings tutorial builds exactly this (0.75 scale, AspectRatio 2.5, MaxSize 800, MinSize 350, fill at 0.25) and the wireframing chapter tells you to test legibility against varied backgrounds — translucency is how this genre stays subordinate to the game instead of covering it

transparencyLadder.rule: depth is expressed as steps on this ladder; a container that only arranges children carries no fill at all
transparencyLadder.why: the Laser Tag HUD uses precisely these values and nothing else to separate its layers, which is why that HUD reads as calm — a neutral theme that reaches for a second accent colour where a transparency step would do has already stopped being neutral

panelStroke.rule: a soft separating edge, present so the surface reads against any background — never the identifying feature
panelStroke.why: the settings tutorial's stroke is thickness 3 in black at 0.25 transparency and nothing in these references uses a stroke as decoration; the staff post also notes UIStroke has no scale support, so a heavy stroke authored on desktop becomes a crayon border on a phone

textStroke.instead: white text on a dark translucent surface, with contrast supplied by the surface
textStroke.why: not one of the eleven references applies an outline to text in a neutral UI, and the Laser Tag HUD gets its legibility from pure white on a 0.15–0.25 backing instead — copying the simulator's 2px text stroke into this theme is the single most likely way to make it look wrong

header.rule: the title is text inside the panel, larger and bolder than body text, separated by padding; weight carries it, not a separate object
header.why: Roblox's design guidance says headers 'should be larger and bolder than body text' and the Laser Tag screens set hierarchy with Montserrat Medium/Bold/Black at LayoutOrder -1 — there is no plaque anywhere in this genre, so a generator that reaches for the simulator's overhanging banner produces a costume, not a theme

closeButton.sizeRule: 0.15 of the panel, 1:1 aspect constraint, capped at 44px
closeButton.why: the settings tutorial anchors close at (1,0) and positions it at (1,-10,0,10) with ImageTransparency 0.25 — a quiet glyph inset inside the corner is the neutral form, and the red circle proud of the corner belongs to the cartoon genres and would read as a different product entirely

spacing.rule: group by proximity and separate by empty space; do not draw divider lines between grouped rows
spacing.why: the Laser Tag layouts express every gap in scale (0.025–0.035) with 2–3% screen margins, and Roblox's guidance says elements surrounded by ample negative space are the eye-catching ones — in this genre padding is the emphasis mechanism that colour is in the others

typography.rule: one family, three weights; scale text with TextScaled plus a UITextSizeConstraint, or with AutomaticSize when the player's text-size setting must be honoured
typography.why: the curriculum uses one family and exactly these three weights, the size-modifiers reference states outright not to set MinTextSize below 9, and the accessibility page notes TextScaled elements do NOT respond to PreferredTextSize — so which scaling mechanism is chosen is an accessibility decision, not a styling one

buttonStates.hover: UIScale nudge and/or a GuiState Hover style rule — the modifier scales children and strokes with it
buttonStates.pressed: swap the image or step the fill one rung down the transparency ladder
buttonStates.rule: the control must be housed in a container (fill, border or background) so it reads as pressable at rest
buttonStates.why: Roblox's guidance names hover, depressed and released (selected) as the requirement and states that unaffordable prices display in red; the Laser Tag buttons fade to 0.65 rather than greying out, which keeps a disabled control legible instead of turning it into a smudge

motion.easing: Exponential for chrome, a single overshoot at most for the panel itself
motion.reducedMotion: when GuiService.ReducedMotionEnabled is true, set TweenInfo.Time to 0 or replace movement with a fade
motion.why: the settings tutorial opens over 0.5s and closes instantly, which is the asymmetry that makes a menu feel responsive rather than slow, and the accessibility page gives the exact reduced-motion substitution — motion that cannot be turned off is a defect in this genre

screenRegions.centre: the action focal point (reticle, cast bar, prompt)
screenRegions.topLeft: RESERVED — Roblox experience controls, left-aligned, dynamic width, can span the full width in portrait
screenRegions.topRight: the creator's own chrome, because Roblox states it left that side free
screenRegions.why: the wireframing chapter assigns these categories by region and the experience-controls announcement says the right side was deliberately left to creators; the three reserved corners are not style opinions, they are occupied space, and UI placed there is unreachable on a phone

safeArea.screenInsets: CoreUISafeInsets (the ScreenGui default) for ordinary UI; TopbarSafeInsets only for something that must live in the top bar row
safeArea.topbarHeightPx: read it at runtime from GuiService.TopbarInset or GuiService:GetInsetArea — do not hardcode
safeArea.topbarHeightDisputed: the staff post says an offset height of 36; a reply in the same thread says 58 in current clients
safeArea.reactToWidth: subscribe to the width-change signal, because the controls resize as features toggle
safeArea.why: two Roblox sources give two different top bar heights, which is the argument for reading the inset rather than trusting either number, and the default ScreenInsets already solves the common case — most 'my UI is behind the topbar' construction is undone by leaving the default alone

layering.rule: each modal or overlay is its own ScreenGui with a higher DisplayOrder; ZIndex and LayoutOrder order things WITHIN one container
layering.resetOnSpawn: set false explicitly on any persistent HUD
layering.why: the containers reference states DisplayOrder layers whole ScreenGuis and that ResetOnSpawn defaults to true — a HUD that vanishes on respawn is the classic symptom of neither being set

iconography.rule: square, held by UIAspectRatioConstraint, ScaleType Fit, authored white so a Color3 can tint them; icons in one stat family share palette and silhouette
iconography.never: an icon carrying meaning that no symbol or label repeats
iconography.why: the curriculum constrains every icon to 1:1 and uses white source art for runtime tinting, and the accessibility page requires symbols alongside colour because colour alone excludes over 5% of players

grid.rule: a neutral list is full-width rows with an icon at the left, a label block, and the value or action at the right; when a grid is genuinely needed it is 3 across with square tiles, not 4
grid.why: the neutral theme's own row in ui-kit-themes.ts declares layout 'rows', and nothing in these references packs dense tile walls the way the simulator sources do — restraint here means fewer, wider, more legible rows

themeSystem.rule: emit one token StyleSheet (colour, radius, spacing, type), a theme sheet deriving from it, a design sheet of StyleRules, and a single StyleLink on the ScreenGui
themeSystem.selectors: class, .Tag, instance name, ::UICorner modifier, GuiState (Hover), @Query for screen size / input / accessibility
themeSystem.why: the styling docs state only one StyleSheet applies per tree and that a token referenced as $Name can feed BackgroundColor3, TextColor3 and UIStroke.Color at once — a restrained theme survives only if its restraint is declared in one place rather than repeated per element, which is also what makes it re-themeable later

genres.label: Survival / crafting — hotbars, needs meters, crafting panes, base-building placement
demonstrates: the HUD is a SET of stacked bars — health, stamina, hunger, thirst, and a level bar — read and judged as one component, not as five independent widgets

the first critique in the thread is a PARITY failure: health and stamina had a colour 'leak'/glow treatment and hunger and thirst did not, and a reviewer noticed the two missing ones before anything else
the fix accepted by the reviewer was not to remove the glow but to give the missing bars the same treatment, rendered pixelated to match the game's art register
five tool slots numbered 1-5 sit at the bottom; two MENU buttons numbered 6-7 sit beside them but deliberately OFFSET from the row

a reviewer asked why 6 and 7 were misaligned — the author had to explain the offset was intentional and that icons would be added, which is the proof that an unoffset, unlabelled neighbour reads as a sixth and seventh item slot
the stated success criterion is legibility under stress: 'easy to read' during high-pressure play, not attractiveness at rest

the governing rule for slot typography, stated explicitly: emphasis is proportional to how often a value CHANGES — 'the slot numbers should have less emphasis than the counter because the former is the information that changes the least often'
so the keybind digit is small and pushed to a corner, and the stack count is the large glyph on the tile

three shipped comparisons are named to support it: World of Warcraft puts keybinds in a corner with minimal emphasis and item counts prominently at the bottom of the slot; Minecraft omits slot numbers entirely; TERA sets slot and item numbers at similar size but gives the centre of the box to the value that moves (cooldown/reload)
the corollary a generator must apply: the slot's centre belongs to the item, the corner to the static keybind, and the largest type to whatever is counting down or counting up
the redesign MOVED the hotbar from bottom-left to bottom-CENTRE, and that relocation is presented as the improvement, not as a preference
a stamina bar tucked beside the hotbar drew repeated complaints for being unlabelled — multiple reviewers could not identify what it measured
the bar's thinness was itself cited as the reason it could not be labelled, so a meter too short to carry an icon or a word is a construction error, not a styling one
the bar's hue (purple-pink) against the hotbar's fill was called 'hard to see or uncomfortable to look at', i.e. a meter's colour must be chosen against its NEIGHBOUR, not in isolation
'out of the way' was used as a criticism — a meter separated from the other meters loses its meaning even when it is perfectly drawn
the survival screen is THREE simultaneous regions, not one modal: hotbar along the bottom, 'Backpack' panel on the LEFT, 'Hand Crafting' panel on the RIGHT
the two panels carry literal word titles ('Backpack', 'Hand Crafting') rather than icons alone
item counts are written on the tile in the form 'Wood x 1', and a bare stack number '999' is the other form used

reviewers asked for the count text to be plain white and the panel titles to be a lighter tint of the panel material with a drop shadow — the numeral and the title are deliberately different treatments
multiple independent reviewers asked for a SEARCH field in the crafting pane, which is the recurring demand once a recipe list grows past what one screen shows
the material register reviewers pushed toward is dark and brown — they named Raft and Muck by title — not the saturated candy palette of the simulator genre
the author's own check was cross-monitor legibility: it looked cramped at Studio size and read correctly at 27-inch and 15-inch play sizes
final layout is two-pane: a scrollable LIST of craftable items on the left, a detail pane on the right
reading order inside the detail pane was deliberately changed to name-above-requirements, with ingredients read left to right
the requirement block is a GRID of ingredient chips, not a single line of text, specifically so a recipe with many ingredients does not overflow one line
the label was shortened from 'Materials Needed:' to 'Requires:' to buy space while staying explicit — the word was kept, not replaced by an icon
for positional recipes the selected recipe paints TRANSPARENT ghost ingredients into the empty crafting slots, described by the author as 'a bit like in Minecraft'
critique that shaped it: list rows were 'quite thick', and both text size and inter-row padding were reduced

the stated accessibility principle is that every section carries an explicit title because 'players don't know what to do without guides' — nothing in a crafting pane may be discoverable only by trial
the meter is a ROW OF PIPS with discrete art states rather than a continuously filling track
hunger runs Full / Half / Empty — three states per pip, so a pip is worth two units of resolution, not one
health does NOT reuse hunger's states: it runs Intact / Cracked / Broken, i.e. damage is drawn as damage to the icon rather than as absence of the icon
the depleted state is drawn (a minimal or broken glyph), never simply hidden — the row's length is constant as the value falls
colour carries the state alongside the drawing: vibrant when full, desaturated as it empties, so the meter survives being read in peripheral vision
the radial meter is the survival genre's alternative to a bar, and it is built, not drawn: two half-circle frames with ClipDescendants and a rotating UIGradient
the mapping is exact and reusable: each degree of rotation equals 3.6 units of a 0-100 value, i.e. 3.6 degrees per percent
the two halves are driven by clamped expressions — the right half by math.min(valueInDegrees, -180), the left by math.max(valueInDegrees + 180, 0) — so one value drives both without a seam
the rejected alternative is on record: 99 duplicated pizza-slice images rotated 3.6 degrees each, which works and is dismissed as the heavy way
a reviewer called the un-eased transition 'rough'; the accepted fix is to TWEEN the driving value rather than to set it, so a radial meter that jumps is a defect
the ring's radius never changes — only the gradient's rotation does

rules.note: Units: px for pixel geometry, studs for world placement, degrees for rotation, and RATIOS where no image was measured. Every value here is either (a) a published default from a fetched module, marked measured:true, or (b) a relationship stated by an author or reviewer, expressed as a ratio and marked derived:true. Nothing is a remembered pixel. Colour is not construction and is deliberately almost absent; the one colour rule below is about legibility against a neighbour, not about a palette.

meterStack.layout: one vertical stack of horizontal tracks, all the same length, in ONE screen corner
meterStack.why: every fetched survival HUD presents the needs meters as a single component and is criticised as one: the feedback thread's bars are judged together, and a stamina bar that sat apart from its siblings was called 'out of the way' and became unreadable despite being correctly drawn. Scattering meters across the screen is the genre's most common construction failure.

meterTreatmentParity.rule: whatever treatment one meter has — glow, bevel, outline, texture, end cap — EVERY meter in the stack has, identically
meterTreatmentParity.never: giving health and stamina a finished treatment and leaving hunger and thirst plain
meterTreatmentParity.why: this exact asymmetry was the first thing a reviewer named in the survival HUD thread, before layout or colour, and the accepted fix was to add the missing treatment rather than to strip the existing one. An odd meter out does not read as restraint, it reads as unfinished.

meterIdentity.rule: every meter carries its own icon or word at the leading end of the track, outside the fill; hue alone never identifies a meter
meterIdentity.minTrackHeightForIcon: a track too short to seat an icon or a label is too short, full stop
meterIdentity.why: an unlabelled stamina bar drew repeated 'what is that' replies, and the author's own excuse was that the bar was too thin to label — which makes the thinness the defect. Two meters in the same HUD differ by one glyph, not by two hues a player must learn.

meterColourAgainstNeighbour.rule: a meter's fill is chosen against the surface it sits on and the meters beside it, not from a palette in isolation
meterColourAgainstNeighbour.why: the one colour critique that survived review was relational: purple-pink over a bright orange-yellow hotbar was called hard to see and uncomfortable, and the suggested replacement was picked for contrast against that neighbour. This is the only colour rule in this file because colour is otherwise not construction.

meterDepletion.rule: the track's LENGTH is constant; only the fill inside it changes. The empty remainder stays drawn as a darker trough
meterDepletion.never: shrinking the whole widget as the value falls
meterDepletion.why: holds across all three meter forms observed: the bar keeps its track, the pip row keeps every pip and draws the empty ones as minimal or broken glyphs, and the radial keeps its full ring and rotates a gradient inside it. A widget that shrinks stops being comparable against itself a second later.

radialMeter.construction: two half-circle frames with ClipDescendants, one rotating UIGradient each, driven by a single 0-100 value
radialMeter.easing: tween the driving value, never set it
radialMeter.why: this is the published working construction for the genre's circular hunger/oxygen meter, and the 3.6-degrees-per-percent mapping plus the two clamped halves are quoted from it. The un-tweened version was called 'rough' by a reviewer, so the easing is part of the construction rather than a polish pass.

discreteMeter.rule: when the meter is a row of pips, each pip has THREE states and the depleted state is drawn, not hidden
discreteMeter.never: reusing one pip artwork for both meters
discreteMeter.why: taken from a posted texture sheet where hunger empties and health BREAKS — damage is drawn as damage to the glyph, not as absence of it. Half states double a pip row's resolution, which is why ten pips can stand in for a hundred-point value.

hotbar.why: nine slots is the count a published survival framework ships; bottom-centre is the relocation a hotbar redesign made and presented as the fix, replacing bottom-left. Square slots are what every tiled hotbar in the fetched threads uses, and a non-square slot immediately reads as a list row.

hotbarLabelWeight.keybind: small, in a corner of the slot
hotbarLabelWeight.stackCount: the large glyph, in the opposite corner
hotbarLabelWeight.centre: belongs to the item, or to whatever is counting
hotbarLabelWeight.why: the explicit stated rule is that emphasis is proportional to how often a value changes: the keybind never changes and the count changes constantly. Three shipped games were named in support — keybinds in corners with minimal emphasis, counts prominent, and in one case slot numbers omitted altogether. The ratio is the smallest that makes the relationship visible rather than a measured value.

hotbarNeighbours.rule: menu or utility buttons placed beside the hotbar must be separated by a gap of at least one slot width AND carry an icon rather than a number
hotbarNeighbours.never: continuing the numbering (…5, 6, 7) into buttons that are not item slots
hotbarNeighbours.why: a survival HUD did exactly that and the first reviewer question was why buttons 6 and 7 were misaligned — meaning the offset alone did not stop them reading as slots six and seven. The number is what makes a tile an item slot; take the number away and add the icon.

panelTriad.layout: three simultaneous regions — hotbar bottom-centre, inventory/backpack on one side, crafting on the other
panelTriad.never: collapsing inventory and crafting into one centred modal
panelTriad.titles: each panel carries a word title, not an icon alone
panelTriad.why: this is where the survival genre parts company with the simulator genre, which centres a single modal over the world. A shipped survival UI put 'Backpack' left and 'Hand Crafting' right with the hotbar between them, because crafting is a transfer between two open surfaces and a modal hides the one you are dragging from.

inventoryCapacity.rule: the inventory header shows the capacity as a readable number, and when the game weighs items it shows BOTH the slot count and the carry weight
inventoryCapacity.placement: in the panel header, always visible, never only on failure
inventoryCapacity.why: a survival framework governs its inventory by 'slots + carry-weight' together, and a shipped game's own player guide instructs players to read the weight limit BEFORE collecting. A capacity a player learns about by being refused is a capacity the UI failed to show.

itemCountFormat.onTile: the count sits on the item tile itself, not in a separate column
itemCountFormat.treatment: plain light numerals; the panel TITLE gets the decorated treatment, the numeral does not
itemCountFormat.why: both forms were used in a shipped survival UI, and reviewers asked specifically for white count text while pushing the panel titles toward a tinted, shadowed treatment — the number is for reading fast and the title is for finding the panel, so they are deliberately not the same object.

craftingLayout.right: detail pane: name on top, then the requirement block, then the craft action
craftingLayout.rowDensity: tight — list rows were explicitly thinned and their padding reduced under review
craftingLayout.why: the two-pane list-plus-detail arrangement is where an iterated crafting menu landed after critique, and the reading order was deliberately rearranged to put the name above the requirements. A grid of recipe cards was not what survived review; a list was.

ingredientRequirement.rule: requirements are a GRID of ingredient chips, each chip an icon plus a have/need pair, under a short explicit label
ingredientRequirement.label: Requires:
ingredientRequirement.never: a single line of comma-separated text
ingredientRequirement.why: the grid was adopted precisely so a recipe with many ingredients does not overflow one line, and the label was shortened from 'Materials Needed:' to buy space while keeping the word — the author's stated principle is that every section is explicitly titled because players will not discover a crafting pane by trial.

recipeGhostHint.rule: for a positional recipe, paint transparent ghost ingredients into the empty crafting slots of the selected recipe
recipeGhostHint.never: leaving the slots blank and expecting the player to know the arrangement
recipeGhostHint.why: described by the menu's author as the fix that made positional crafting teachable, 'a bit like in Minecraft'. The ghost is the only thing in the pane that says where an ingredient goes, and without it a positional grid is a guessing game.

recipeSearch.rule: a crafting pane whose list is longer than one screen gets a search field in its header
recipeSearch.why: multiple independent reviewers of the same shipped survival UI asked for it, and the author's only reason for deferring was scripting time, not disagreement. It is the one crafting feature that was requested by more than one person in the same thread.

placementMode.rule: building is a MODE with its own input map and its own on-screen key hints, entered from the build menu and exited explicitly
placementMode.why: these are the published defaults of an open-source placement module, and they are invisible without a hint strip. The crafting thread's own accessibility finding — that players do not discover functionality without being told — applies with more force here, because a placement mode with hidden keys traps the player in it.

placementPreview.ghost: a translucent clone of the object, snapped to the grid, eased toward the cursor rather than teleported
placementPreview.validityChannel: tint the ENTIRE preview one colour, recomputed every frame
placementPreview.footprint: drawn by a separate bounding-box object, not by the tint
placementPreview.why: the lerp speed and the two-colour tint are published module defaults, and a second independent placement class exposes the same pair as configurable validPlacementColors / invalidPlacementColors — two modules agreeing makes it a convention rather than one author's habit. Validity as a tint and footprint as a box are separate visuals in both.

placementGrid.gridVisualisation: point markers at each grid node, shown during placement and switchable off
placementGrid.why: 1 stud and 15 degrees are the published defaults of a fetched placement module; the point-marker visualisation and the plot-relative rotation come from a second one, which keeps snapping correct on rotated and inverted plots. Quantised rotation is what stops a base looking hand-thrown.

dayNightReadout.format: abbreviated day name, then a zero-padded 12-hour clock with AM/PM — e.g. 'Sun 12:00 PM'
dayNightReadout.source: Lighting:GetMinutesAfterMidnight(), converted — never an independent timer
dayNightReadout.why: this is the implementation that answered the question in the fetched thread, and the negative half matters more than the positive: it has NO icon, NO dial and NO progress bar. A generator's reflex is to invent a sun-and-moon arc; nothing observed here does that, and driving the label from Lighting rather than a separate timer is what keeps the readout from disagreeing with the sky.

materialRegister.rule: survival panels read as MATERIAL — dark, desaturated, wood and earth — while the simulator genre reads as candy. Same construction discipline, different substance
materialRegister.why: the only art-direction note that reviewers of a shipped survival UI converged on, naming Raft and Muck as the target. Recorded as a register rather than as a palette, because this library's founding lesson is that getting the colours right while getting the construction wrong produces the near-miss that started it.

legibilityUnderStress.rule: the survival HUD's acceptance test is reading it mid-fight at play size, not admiring it at rest in Studio
legibilityUnderStress.why: stated by a reviewer as the compliment that mattered — 'easy to read' in high-stress situations — and independently by an author who found the same UI cramped at Studio scale and correct at 15-inch and 27-inch play sizes. A survival HUD is checked while something is chasing you or nothing about it has been checked.

genres.label: Tower defense / unit-placement defense (TD, anime-TD, wave defense)
demonstrates: the in-match HUD is THREE readouts and nothing else competing with them: base health, current wave, wave timer — and they are one assembly, not three widgets. The wiki describes it as a single bar: 'The main bar is the amount of health you have... The left text is the current wave. The right text is the remaining amount of time for the wave to end/wave to start.'
base health is a NUMBER on a bar, default 100, and the number is mutable by perks and by map modifiers (a shown example reads 200) — so the bar must render an arbitrary max, never a hardcoded 100

skip-wave is a VOTE BOX that appears after a delay, with accept and decline, and a tally in 'cast/required' form — '0/2 means that 0 players have voted to skip the wave and 2 players are required' — not a plain Skip button

the tower hotbar is the LOADOUT, fixed at five slots (six in some events, fewer in some modes), and 'Each slot has a number in the top left corner, which shows which key on the keyboard you have to press to place down your towers' — the keybind digit is a badge in the slot's top-left, not a caption underneath

clicking a placed tower opens an upgrade box whose contents are, in order: the NEXT upgrade's name, level and icon plus the changes it brings; detection badges for hidden / lead / flying arranged AROUND the tower icon; a progress bar under the upgrade name showing how many upgrades remain (three to six depending on the tower); the upgrade cost ON the button, greyed out at last level
sell is a button carrying the refund AMOUNT, and the targeting selector sits immediately next to it with seven fixed modes — First (default), Last, Strongest, Weakest, Closest, Farthest, Random

under the tower's model preview in that same box sit three lifetime figures: total damage dealt, current level, total cash spent on the tower; current stats (damage, firerate, range, income) run down the RIGHT side of the box

placement legality is signalled in the 3D world, not in the UI: 'You can only place towers down if their primary range circle is white', other towers project red spots, and cliff spots highlight while a cliff tower is held

a tower can carry more than one range circle at once: white primary range, a RED deadzone circle that enemies inside cannot be targeted from (Rocketeer), and additional ORANGE circles for utility ranges (Necromancer, Engineer)
match modifiers render as a small icon row at the bottom-left of the screen
keybinds are the interaction, not a convenience: 1-6 pick a tower, Q cancel placement, R rotate placement, E upgrade, T upgrade the tower's bottom path, X sell, Q switch hotbar, F/B/H/J/K/L abilities
mobile is the SAME HUD plus a joystick, jump, run, emote and sticker buttons — the TD layout is not re-flowed for touch, it is augmented; and 'you need to double tap to select and place down towers'
the pre-match screen is a mode VOTE with a ready button under the modes that shortens the timer to five seconds, not a menu
game speed is a set of DISCRETE STOPS, never a slider: 0x (full pause), 0.5x, 1x, 1.5x, 2x, with 1x the default

0x is a first-class stop and is described as a reading aid — 'pauses the match entirely, preventing anything from moving, which can be useful to allow more time to react'. A speed control that only goes forward is missing half of what the convention is for.
the control is ENTITLEMENT-GATED and consumes a currency (Time Scale Tickets) — so the speed cluster needs a locked/unavailable state and a cost affordance, not just five toggles
background music is explicitly exempt from the time scale, so the control is a simulation-rate control and not an audio-rate control
with the Sandbox Plus+ gamepass the scale can be set to custom values beyond 2x — the ladder has an unbounded variant, so the widget should not hardcode five children

the keybind badge is bounded by the keyboard, not by the rail: 'any towers selected past the 6th will not have a hotkey, and will have to be placed by clicking their button' — slots 7+ render with no digit badge rather than with a fake one

the admin/sandbox surface is a left SIDEBAR of toggles over the live board (infinite cash, infinite towers, invincible, consumable cooldowns, time scale) — a TD config surface is a rail beside the match, never a modal that hides the path
the entity picker is split into named sections (Modern / Legacy) and hovering an entry surfaces its health and speed as a hover readout
right-click on an icon in the picker is the add/remove-from-loadout gesture, distinct from left-click which selects
desktop placement is a two-step gesture: click the unit tile, DRAG the ghost across the map, click to commit — the ghost tracks the cursor between the two clicks
the same hotbar key or the same tile, pressed a second time, is the CANCEL — cancellation is the selection gesture repeated, not a separate control

touch placement is a different interaction and needs different chrome: after tapping the unit and tapping the ground, 'you will see two options on the right of the screen (Place and Cancel)'. An explicit confirm/cancel PAIR appears on the RIGHT edge on touch and does not exist on desktop.
hotbar digits are 1 through 6 — the same six-slot ceiling as TDS, from an unrelated studio

the placed-tower surface is described as a CARD, not a window: 'When clicking/tapping on a tower, a card appears, which allows you to sell, upgrade, and see your tower's stats' — sell, upgrade and stats are the three obligatory regions

placement surfaces are typed and mutually exclusive: 'some units can only be placed on the ground, while others must be placed on high ground', so the legality tint has to answer a per-unit rule and not a global one
the loadout is six slots with the FIRST slot semantically special (leader), carrying a party-wide buff — the rail has a distinguished first cell rather than six identical cells
upgrades change abilities, not only numbers, so the upgrade card must have room for a named ability that is replaced, not merely a stat delta
the placement preview is a CLONE of the real tower model with a dedicated 'Collider' part at Transparency 0.5 — the ghost is the actual model made translucent, not a silhouette or an icon

validity is signalled by TINTING that collider: a green (BrickColor 'Sage green') fill for placeable and a red ('Really red') fill for blocked. The tint lives on the ghost, in the world, not as a banner in the ScreenGui.
minimum tower-to-tower spacing is enforced as a magnitude test — the thread's value is 6 studs — and breaching it is what flips the ghost red, so the red state has a spatial cause the player can see
placement is restricted to designated surfaces by name (a 'PlacePart'), so the buildable area is authored geometry and the ghost is legal only over it
left click commits, RIGHT CLICK cancels — the desktop cancel is the opposite mouse button, matching the keyboard cancel rather than replacing it
the range indicator is a 3D MESH lying on the ground, not a UI circle: a circular mesh of 65 vertices and 64 bones, one bone per sampled angle
64 segments is the practical fidelity ceiling — the author states it 'gets less precise after 64' — so a range ring is a 64-gon, and a radius parameter scales it rather than a new mesh being built

the ring can be occlusion-aware: raycasting outward along each bone and pulling bones inward where geometry blocks the shot turns the circle into the tower's actual reachable area rather than a decorative disc
glow is faked with a larger Neon clone behind the mesh, because Roblox will not render a Highlight over a transparent mesh — the outline has to be geometry or texture, it cannot be a stroke

the striped disc under a TDS tower is 'a cylinder with a texture on it' — the circular base marker is world geometry with a tiled texture, which is why it sits under the tower in perspective instead of floating flat like a ScreenGui frame

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units — px for stroke and radius, studs for world distances, scale-relative for placement. Anything inherited from simulator.json rather than observed for this genre is marked inherited:true, because a rule nobody checked in this genre is a guess wearing a number.

hudTriad.rule: The in-match HUD is exactly three readouts, and base health, wave number and wave timer are ONE assembly, not three widgets: a health bar across the top centre with the wave number set at its LEFT end and the countdown at its RIGHT end.
hudTriad.never: three separate corner-anchored panels for health, wave and timer
hudTriad.why: TDS describes the whole thing as 'the main bar' with left text and right text. Splitting it into three corners is the single most common way a generated TD HUD stops reading as a TD HUD.

cashReadout.rule: Match cash is its own pill, separate from the health/wave assembly, and is the value the tower rail and every cost label are compared against.
cashReadout.position: near the tower rail, not in the health assembly
cashReadout.why: Cash changes on every kill and every purchase; parking it inside the wave bar makes the one number the player watches while placing sit at the opposite end of the screen from the rail they are placing from.

towerRail.rule: A horizontal rail of square tower tiles along the BOTTOM of the screen. Slot count is the LOADOUT size, fixed for the match — five or six — not the size of the player's inventory.
towerRail.costLabel: every tile carries its placement cost
towerRail.why: TDS (five slots, digit in the top-left corner), ASTD (six, first slot is the leader) and Toilet Tower Defense (bottom rail, cost per tile) agree across three studios. TDS also states outright that slots past the sixth get NO hotkey, so slot 7+ renders with no badge rather than a fabricated one.

affordability.rule: An unaffordable tile DIMS and its cost label goes red; the tile is never removed, never reordered, and never hidden.
affordability.why: Toilet Tower Defense opens with 300 against a rail most of whose tiles cost more. The rail's job early in a match is to show the player what they are saving toward, so the unaffordable state is the default state and must stay legible.

placementPreview.rule: The preview is a CLONE of the real tower model with its collider at Transparency 0.5, following the pointer ray. Validity is a TINT ON THE GHOST — green placeable, red blocked — never a banner, toast or text warning in the ScreenGui.
placementPreview.surfaceIsAuthored: placement is legal only over named buildable geometry, and the legality rule is per-tower-type (ground vs cliff/high-ground)
placementPreview.why: The DevForum placement system tints a 0.5-transparency collider sage green / really red at a 6-stud spacing test; TDS states placement is legal only while the primary range circle is white and that other towers project red spots. Two independent sources put the answer in the world, on the model. A generated TD that prints 'Invalid placement' in a label has moved the feedback to where the player is not looking.

placementGesture.desktop: click the tile (or press its digit) → ghost follows the cursor → LEFT CLICK commits
placementGesture.desktopCancel: right click, the Q key, or pressing the same tile/digit a second time — all three cancel
placementGesture.touch: tap the tile → tap the ground → an explicit PLACE / CANCEL button pair appears on the RIGHT EDGE of the screen and commits or aborts
placementGesture.why: ASTD documents the re-press-to-cancel gesture and the touch-only Place/Cancel pair on the right; the DevForum system uses right-click to cancel; TDS binds Q to cancel and R to rotate and says mobile requires a double tap. The touch confirm pair is the rule a generator will miss: on touch the commit cannot be the same tap as the aim.

rangeIndicator.rule: The range ring is WORLD GEOMETRY lying on the ground under the tower — a ~64-segment circular mesh, or a cylinder with the ring baked into its texture — not a UI circle and not a Highlight.
rangeIndicator.outline: baked into the texture or built as a larger Neon clone behind the mesh

channels.red: deadzone — enemies inside cannot be targeted
channels.orange: secondary or utility range (buff aura, repair radius)

rangeIndicator.shownWhen: while a tower is held for placement, and while a placed tower is selected
rangeIndicator.engineConstraints: a Highlight will not render over a transparent part, and a place may hold at most 32 Highlights at once — so per-tower selection outlines must be geometry or texture
rangeIndicator.why: The FOV resource is a 65-vertex / 64-bone mesh and says precision stops improving past 64; the TDS-reproduction thread says the disc is a textured cylinder whose outline is part of the image. TDS itself documents three simultaneous ring colours on one tower. A single flat white circle drawn in a ScreenGui fails all three.

upgradePopover.rule: Clicking a placed tower opens a side-anchored CARD, never a centred modal — the path and the enemies must stay visible while the player upgrades.
upgradePopover.anchor: screen edge beside the tower, board stays uncovered
upgradePopover.orientation: vertical, split into an identity/preview region and a stats region
regions: identity: tower name with its rank/tier as a prefix or a corner badge on the name line, and a live model preview
lifetime figures under the preview: total damage dealt, current level, total cash spent on this tower
detection badges — hidden / lead / flying — arranged AROUND the tower icon, not listed as text
next upgrade: its name, its level, its icon and the stat changes it brings
a segmented progress bar of upgrade steps remaining (3-6 steps is the normal range; short ladders of 3 also ship)
current stats down the right side: damage, firerate, range, income — each with a TEXT LABEL beside its icon
the action row: upgrade, sell, targeting
upgradePopover.upgradeList: authored as a SCROLLING region, because the number of upgrade rows varies per tower
upgradePopover.why: TDS's upgrade box is the fullest description found and every region above appears in it; the two DevForum feedback threads independently name the vertical left/right split, the tier-as-prefix resolution, the cut-off upgrade list that needed to scroll, and the icon-only stats nobody could read.

upgradeButton.rule: The upgrade button CARRIES ITS COST as its main text. At max level it greys out in place — it is never removed and never replaced by a different control.
upgradeButton.maxLevelState: greyed, still showing the ladder as complete
upgradeButton.why: TDS: 'The upgrade cost is also shown. You can click it to buy the upgrade. If the tower is on its last level, the upgrade button is greyed out.' A cost-less 'Upgrade' button makes the player open the card to learn a number they should have been able to read from it.

sellButton.rule: Sell carries the REFUND AMOUNT as a number, not the bare word Sell, and sits immediately beside the targeting selector.
sellButton.why: TDS: 'You can sell towers to remove them, but only get the stated amount of money back.' The refund is never the full spend, so the number is the whole decision.

targetingSelector.rule: A cycling selector adjacent to sell, with seven fixed modes in this order: First, Last, Strongest, Weakest, Closest, Farthest, Random. First is the default for every tower.
targetingSelector.why: Enumerated exactly in TDS. This set is a genre convention strong enough that a TD card without it reads as unfinished; inventing a different set reads as a different game.

waveProgression.rule: Waves are numbered from 0 and the inter-wave gap is a live countdown, not a Next Wave button. The early-start affordance is a VOTE BOX with a cast/required tally ('0/2'), offering accept and decline.
waveProgression.why: TDS: the skip box appears after a delay, needs the stated number of votes, and grants the wave reward early at the cost of the next wave starting early. A single-player Skip button drops the whole tension of the mechanic.

speedControl.rule: Discrete stops, never a slider: 0x, 0.5x, 1x, 1.5x, 2x, with 1x pre-selected. 0x is a real stop and is a reading aid, not a pause menu.
speedControl.lockable: the cluster needs a locked/priced state — in TDS it consumes a ticket currency and is solo-only; an unbounded variant exists behind a gamepass, so the widget must not hardcode five children
speedControl.why: Enumerated on the TDS Time Scale page. The 0x stop is the one a generator omits and the one players use most for reading a crowded board.

modifierStrip.rule: Active match modifiers render as a small icon row at the BOTTOM-LEFT of the screen, with the detail on hover.
modifierStrip.why: TDS states the position outright. It is the one HUD region left for per-match state, and it stays out of the rail's way.

configRail.rule: Any in-match configuration surface (admin, sandbox, settings) is a rail down a screen EDGE over the live board, not a modal that hides the path.
configRail.why: The TDS sandbox admin panel is a sidebar of toggles with the match still running behind it. A TD match cannot be paused to read a menu unless the game has an explicit 0x stop, so its menus have to be edge-anchored.

typography.rule: ONE typeface across the entire HUD, every rail tile, every card and every readout. Numbers are the only thing allowed a different weight.
typography.iconography: one kind of icon — either all image assets or all glyphs, never mixed — and every stat icon gets a text label beside it
typography.why: Both DevForum feedback threads led with exactly these two faults. They are also the two faults a generator falls into by default, because it reaches for an emoji when it has no asset.

cardPadding.rule: One uniform gutter inside the upgrade card, applied at the container, not per-element nudges.
cardPadding.why: The GUI-feedback thread records the card reading 'too compact' with the stats title colliding with the upgrade rows, and then the correction over-spacing. Both failures come from spacing set element by element.

panelStroke.why: Inherited from simulator.json, with one genre-specific observation on top: the TDS-reproduction thread describes the panels as 'a box with a UI stroke that has a UIGradient', so in this genre the stroke itself carries a gradient rather than a flat colour. Thickness and colour role are not independently measured here and are carried over.

cornerRadius.why: Inherited from simulator.json. No tower-defense source read here states a radius, so these are carried rather than observed, and say so.

priceDisplay.rule: icon then number inside a pill
priceDisplay.why: Inherited from simulator.json. Consistent with every cost surface described in this genre (tile cost, upgrade cost, sell refund) but not independently measured for stroke or radius here.

genres.label: Tycoon — dropper/conveyor economy, world buy-pads, cash counter, rebirth, plot ownership
demonstrates: the canonical tycoon purchase affordance is described in the thread as stepping on 'a red, squished, cylinder' — a squat floor disc, not a screen button and not a rectangular tile
the pad is a WORLD object the player walks onto; the purchase is made by standing on it, so the pad has to be readable from above and from a distance, not from a cursor hover

the price label above a buy pad is a BillboardGui, and in the working arrangement 'the billboard GUI is inside of the begin working button' — it is a CHILD of the pad, not a sibling floating at a plot coordinate
the label carries name and price on one line in the form quoted in the thread: 'Begin Working! - [$0]' — an imperative or object name, a separator, then the cost bracketed with a currency sign
purchase is expressed by making the pad vanish: the kit 'sets the transparency to 1'
the thread exists because a custom BillboardGui survived that transparency change and kept floating over an empty floor — the label must die with the pad, and parenting is what guarantees it
older kits faked this label with a Humanoid display name before BillboardGui was used for it, which is why some kits still show the label through walls

a buy button pad is composed of exactly three things: 'a transparent part, a BillboardGui showing the price, and an attribute storing the cost and the model it unlocks' — the collision volume, the label and the data are separate and the label reads from the data
on a successful touch the script 'checks the player's cash, deducts the cost, makes the purchased model visible, and destroys the button pad' — reveal and removal are one beat
the cash readout is 'a ScreenGui with a cash display that updates via a RemoteEvent whenever the server modifies the player's balance' — the counter is server-driven and never computed on the client
the server-side truth is leaderstats: 'a folder named leaderstats with an IntValue named Cash inside each player object', which is also what puts every player's cash on Roblox's own player list
plots are attributed by tagging 'each plot with the owning player's UserId'
stated outright: 'destroying the pad after purchase is the visual feedback that the upgrade is done' — the tycoon genre has no owned-state chip, because the bought thing appearing IS the state
the buy handler's own comments name the two visible steps: '-- remove the pad' and '-- reveal + activate the new part'
a `bought` flag guards against the pad firing twice while a player stands on it — a pad is a dwell target, so it needs a latch that a click target would not
cash-carrying drops hold their worth in a Value attribute that the collector reads, so a drop's floating tag can show a real per-item number rather than a fixed one
remaining progress is rendered as a currency: 'ButtonsLeft now displays on the UI like a currency for the Default UI' — buttons-left sits in the same chip row as cash, in the same shape

number rendering is an explicit setting with three modes — 'Modes for Numbers (None, Comma, Suffix)' — so a tycoon HUD is expected to switch from grouped digits to K/M/B suffixes as the economy inflates
cash drops carry their own world tag whose colour is configurable separately for the currency and the amount: 'Setting for the DropTag Currency & Amount Color'
there is a dedicated wayfinding affordance, a 'Find Next Button UI + Setting' — the plot is large enough that the next pad has to be pointed at
'Support for custom UI above each button' — the per-pad billboard is treated as a themeable slot, not a fixed label
a separate 'RebirthUI' exists alongside the plot, plus persistent HUD buttons for Autocollect and DoubleCash, and pads gated on Premium membership

the rebirth panel's copy, quoted from the thread: 'Rebirthing gives you a 1.1x Cash Boost and allows you to buy Rebirth Buttons!' and 'Rebirthing makes you lose all your progress and restart!' — the reward line and the loss line are two separate sentences, and rebirth unlocks a new CLASS of pad on the plot

the corrected layout proposed in the thread is ordered: the benefit sentence, then the rebirth logo with the rebirth count overlaid on it, then the rebirth button, with the warning demoted to secondary text
the panel was rejected as 'cluttered' in its first form — the fix was ordering and demotion, not new colour

critique on type hierarchy: 'The body of the text is slightly too big, it brings less attention to the title and overall doesn't wrap around very well to read properly' — in a rebirth panel the title must out-weigh the body by a clear step

the author defends the look as deliberately conventional — 'Generic was what I was aiming for. It's something people are used to meaning it's good for FTUE' — and a commenter confirms the convention is genre-wide: 'Every tycoon/simulator does this'

the named failure mode, quoted: 'you have rounded boxes on some, rounded boxes with rainbow outline, a circle, a rounded box with no outline' — mixed corner and outline treatments inside one HUD is what makes a tycoon read as assembled rather than designed

the prescribed fix for the two leader tiles: 'put an outline around them, make them evenly sized under the rebirth bar, put the name of the "king" underneath them so it all fits under the rebirth bar, and add an emoji to make it clearer for a younger audience'
the leader tiles hang UNDER the rebirth progress bar, so the HUD stack is: progress bar first, server-leader tiles beneath it, aligned to its width
label copy is cut to the noun — 'Cash King' rather than 'TheCashKing is' — and spacing defects were called out at the character level ('no space after `Rebirth Progress:`')
the left-edge panel rail was told to standardise its panel sizes; a rail of unequal panels reads as broken even when each panel is fine

too many pads visible at once is a design defect, quoted: 'there are so many upgrade buttons on the plot, it makes it look a bit messy and cramped' — the reviewer's fix is to reveal upgrades progressively rather than all at once
new players could not find the first dropper pad at all, and the arrow indicator meant to point at it was ineffective — the wayfinding affordance is load-bearing, not decoration
the rebirth frame and the party frame were both judged too small; meta panels in a tycoon are routinely undersized relative to the world behind them
text instructions alone did not carry the first-time experience — the plot has to show the next action, not describe it

plot ownership is expressed by the claim door's own material state, not by a panel: unclaimed it is fully opaque and solid; for the owner the reviewed code sets 'claimDoor.Transparency = 0.6' and 'claimDoor.CanCollide = false'
a partially transparent, walk-through door is the readable 'yours' signal — the door stays visible so the plot boundary is still drawn
ownership itself is stored as the owner's UserId in a value object, with no GUI showing a name — which is exactly the gap a generated tycoon should close by putting the owner's name on the door
non-owners are blocked physically by the same door that the owner walks through, so one object carries both the permission and its display

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Tycoon's defining property is that the SHOP IS THE WORLD: purchases happen on pads standing on the plot, and the screen UI is reserved for meta (rebirth, stats, codes, shop). A generator that renders a tycoon as a screen-space item grid has built a simulator with a conveyor in it. Units are Roblox UI units. Where a number could not be observed from a text source it is marked unmeasured rather than invented — see `unmeasured`.

purchaseSurface.rule: a purchase is a world pad the player stands on, placed where the unlocked object will appear
purchaseSurface.never: a screen-space grid of purchasable upgrades as the primary buy flow
purchaseSurface.shape: squat cylinder disc on the floor, height far less than diameter
purchaseSurface.why: the kit convention is described as stepping on 'a red, squished, cylinder'; siting the pad at the build location makes the plot double as a site plan of the finished base

padLabel.container: BillboardGui parented to (or adorned to) the pad part itself
padLabel.content: object name, then the cost with a currency sign
padLabel.lines: name above, price beneath is the safer two-line form; the one-line 'name - [$price]' is what the kits ship
padLabel.why: documented guidance is TextScaled plus a UIAspectRatioConstraint so the price stays readable at every camera distance; parenting to the pad is what makes the label die with it

purchasedState.rule: destroy the pad and its label together; the revealed object is the confirmation
purchasedState.never: leave the pad in place marked OWNED, greyed or disabled
purchasedState.why: stated outright in the template guide — 'destroying the pad after purchase is the visual feedback that the upgrade is done'. This is the exact INVERSE of the simulator rule, where the price is replaced by the word OWNED and the card stays. A generator must not carry the simulator rule across.
purchasedState.commonDefect: a label that is a sibling rather than a child survives the purchase and floats over empty floor — the single most reported tycoon UI bug

padLatch.rule: a pad is a dwell target, so it needs a bought/debounce latch before it fires
padLatch.why: a player standing on a pad re-fires Touched continuously; a click target does not have this problem and a generator that treats the pad as a button will double-charge

affordability.rule: evaluate per player and express it on the pad BODY with a colour swap, and on any screen-space purchase control with a lock icon beside the price
affordability.never: hide or blank the price when it cannot be afforded
affordability.why: the pad body is what the red/green thread recolours; the lock-beside-price form comes from the guidance reference. The specific colour-to-meaning mapping was NOT observed and is left to the theme.

padDensity.rule: reveal pads progressively — a tier's pads appear only when the tier before it is bought
padDensity.never: every pad on the plot visible from the first second
padDensity.why: 'there are so many upgrade buttons on the plot, it makes it look a bit messy and cramped' was the headline critique of a published tycoon; MaxDistance on the billboards handles the rest

wayfinding.rule: ship a persistent 'find next pad' affordance that points at the cheapest unbought pad
wayfinding.why: a shipped kit carries a 'Find Next Button UI' as a named feature, and the one published tycoon reviewed here failed its first-time experience because players could not find the first dropper and the arrow meant to point at it did not work

cashCounter.typeface: monospace or otherwise tabular so the digits do not jitter as they tick
cashCounter.changeFeedback: a brief scale-up, 1.0 to 1.05 and back, on each increment
cashCounter.source: server-driven via RemoteEvent off leaderstats; never computed client-side
cashCounter.why: the counter is the one number a tycoon player watches for minutes at a time, so it must not reflow or flash

numberFormat.escalation: switch to K/M/B suffixes once the value stops fitting the counter's width
numberFormat.why: shipped kits expose exactly these three modes as a setting, because a tycoon economy inflates by orders of magnitude within one session

progressCounter.rule: render remaining purchases ('Buttons Left') as a chip in the same row and the same shape as the currency chips
progressCounter.why: a shipped kit states it plainly — 'ButtonsLeft now displays on the UI like a currency' — because buttons-left, not cash, is the tycoon's actual completion meter

dropTag.rule: a cash drop carries its own world tag showing currency icon and amount, with the currency and the amount coloured separately
dropTag.why: the drop tag is a configurable pair of colours in a shipped kit; the amount comes from the drop's own Value attribute, so the tag shows a real per-item number rather than a constant

order: server-leader tiles beneath it, aligned to its width
hudStack.leaderTiles: equal size, outlined, name underneath, an icon or emoji on each
hudStack.railRule: every panel in the left rail is the same width
hudStack.why: this is the arrangement prescribed to fix a shipped tycoon's HUD; unequal rail panels read as broken even when each panel is fine on its own

panelConsistency.rule: one corner treatment and one outline treatment across every panel in the HUD
panelConsistency.never: rounded boxes on some, rounded-with-outline on others, a circle, and a rounded box with no outline
panelConsistency.why: quoted verbatim as the reason a shipped tycoon's UI read as 'a lot of different UIs mashed together'. This is the tycoon-specific restatement of the simulator library's one-visual-language finding.

order: one row: rebirth button on the LEFT, rebirth emblem with the count overlaid on the RIGHT
loss warning, smaller, below the row
rebirthPanel.copyShape: one sentence for what is gained, one for what is lost, never merged. Write them for THIS game; do not reuse the wording of any kit they were observed in.
rebirthPanel.typeHierarchy: the title must out-weigh the body by a clear step; oversized body text was the named defect
rebirthPanel.unlocks: rebirth opens a new CLASS of pad on the plot, so the panel's promise is spatial and the plot must visibly change
rebirthPanel.sizing: meta panels in tycoons are routinely too small against the world behind them; err large
rebirthPanel.why: A rebirth is the only button in a tycoon that destroys the player's progress on purpose, so the gain and the loss must both be readable before the finger lands. The row pairs the action with the count it will reset, and the warning sits under it in smaller text rather than beside it, where it reads as a caption to the pair instead of a fourth option.

upgradeNode.container: ScrollingFrame of nodes, vertical or grid
upgradeNode.lockedState: dimmed plus a lock icon; unlocked nodes at full colour
upgradeNode.why: a tycoon upgrade is a level on a track, not an item in a shop — the level fraction is what a price pill is in a simulator

statsPanel.why: income per second is the number a tycoon player is actually buying with each pad, and no pad label states it

plotOwnership.rule: ownership is shown on the claim door itself: opaque and solid when unclaimed, semi-transparent and walk-through for the owner
plotOwnership.gap: the reviewed system shows no owner name anywhere — a generated tycoon should put the owner's display name on the door, because the reference proves the slot exists and is empty
plotOwnership.why: one object carries both the permission and its display; the door stays visible so the plot boundary is still drawn

worldUiCulling.rule: set MaxDistance on pad billboards and decide AlwaysOnTop deliberately
worldUiCulling.why: a plot with dozens of pads becomes a wall of overlapping prices without culling; pads behind a built wall should stop competing for attention once AlwaysOnTop is off

saveIndicator.rule: flash a one-second 'Saved' label in a corner after a persistence write
saveIndicator.why: a tycoon session is an hour of accumulation; the player needs to see that it was kept

genres.label: web-landing
demonstrates: A warm near-black page at rgb(20,19,18) with warm off-white text at rgb(244,243,242) — the neutral is warm, not the usual blue-grey, and that is what makes it read as calm rather than cold.

EVERY text node on the page is font-weight 400, including the 96px statement. Hierarchy is carried entirely by size, colour and space, and the absence of bold is the single most distinctive thing about it.
Letter-spacing is negative and proportional to size — about -0.02em, tightening as type grows — and turns POSITIVE (+0.018em) on the 10px uppercase micro labels.

A four-step surface ramp and nothing else: page 20/19/18, raised 23/22/21, card 35/34/33, control 51/50/49, with a single 1px rgb(41,40,39) hairline doing all the separation. Shadows are effectively absent.
One radius does almost all the work: 10px on 343 elements, 6px on 56, pills reserved for buttons.
The nav is 60px, fixed and fully transparent — no blur, no fill — separated from the page by the same hairline as everything else.
The hero's focal object is the product's own input, not a screenshot of it: a large 10px-radius composer sitting on a full-bleed line-art backdrop.
A 1280px container with 32px gutters, and a 7,165px page that is mostly vertical space.
ZERO canvas elements, ZERO <video>, ZERO SVG <animate>. The page the owner pointed at as the example of modern AI-product motion has no ambient animation technique of any kind on it.

138 @keyframes rules are declared, and document.getAnimations() returns 0 while the page sits idle. Every one of those keyframes is a STATE — a toast opening, a skeleton shimmering, a dot pulsing, a sidebar floating in — and none of them is decoration that runs on its own.

Named keyframes read as a catalogue of interaction states rather than scenery: toast-open, toast-close, float-sidebar-in, float-sidebar-out, shimmer-skeleton, pulse-dot, loading-results-shimmer, icon-shimmer, blink, add-top-shadow.

Transition durations cluster in two bands with almost nothing between them: a fast band at 0.1-0.15s (12 elements at 0.15s) for anything under the finger, and a slow band at 0.72s (14 elements) for surfaces that move on their own.
Only 16 elements carry will-change. Compositor hinting is applied to the few things that actually move, not sprayed across the page.
ONE webgl2 canvas, sized 977x485 in the layout, plus ONE autoplaying looping muted <video>. The ambient motion budget is spent on exactly two objects on the whole page.
233 animations were running at the moment of measurement — by far the highest of the five references — against 101 declared @keyframes rules.
A single house transition duration carries the page: 0.2s on 147 separate elements. The next most common is 2s on 26 elements, which is a different job entirely (ambient drift, not response).
A keyframe named canvas-fade-in exists, so the WebGL layer is faded in after it is ready rather than appearing at first paint. The expensive layer is never what the first frame depends on.
Only 13 elements carry will-change, on a page with thousands of elements.
marquee and infinite-scroll keyframes: some of the perceived liveness is continuously scrolling content, not per-element animation.
ZERO canvas, ZERO video, 18 @keyframes rules, 4 animations running. It is the QUIETEST of the five references by a wide margin.
23 of 709 elements carry any transition at all — 3.2%, the lowest ratio measured. Its fast band is 0.1s (9 elements) and 0.15s (5).
A product page can be perceived as modern and expensive while being almost completely still. Stillness is a legitimate position, not a failure state.

TWENTY-NINE <video> elements on one page, and ZERO canvas. Its liveness is moving CONTENT, not a moving background — the page is alive because the product is shown working, over and over, down the length of it.
Only 10 @keyframes rules on a 3,315-element page. Almost no bespoke animation is authored at all.
183 elements carry a transition (5.5%), in two bands: 0.2s on 74 and 0.3s on 54.
The technique that makes this page feel expensive is reach, not sophistication: a long page, and something demonstrating the product in every section of it.

0.rule: One weight. Set every heading and every paragraph at 400 and let size, colour and space carry hierarchy.
0.why: Measured across every text node on the bar: there is no bold anywhere. Reaching for 600 is the reflex that makes a page look like a template, and it is the first thing to go.

1.rule: Warm neutrals only. The page, every surface step and the text all sit on the same warm axis; no blue-grey.
1.why: rgb(20,19,18) against rgb(244,243,242) — red highest, blue lowest, by one or two points at every step. It is barely perceptible per colour and unmistakable across a page.

2.rule: Separate with a 1px hairline, not with a shadow.
2.why: One border colour on the bar and effectively no shadows. Elevation is implied by the surface step, not by a blur.

3.rule: Tighten tracking as type grows; loosen it below 12px.
3.why: -0.02em at 56px and 96px, -0.01em at body, +0.018em on uppercase micro labels. Uniform tracking is what makes large type look rented.

4.rule: A section is a 32px title, a 14–16px muted line, and then the thing itself.
4.why: Repeated at every section on the bar without variation. The consistency is the effect.

5.rule: Never ship a section whose content we cannot fill truthfully.
5.why: Not a rule from the bar — a rule against it. Half its structure is social proof, and an empty or invented version of that is worse than omitting the section.

6.rule: Spend the motion budget on RESPONSE first and scenery last.
6.why: Measured across all four sites the owner named as the bar: ChatGPT has 138 keyframes and zero ambient animation; Grok has 18 keyframes and no canvas or video at all. Not one of the four treats a moving background as the thing that makes a page feel alive, and two of them do not have one.

7.rule: One house transition duration, applied widely, beats several tuned ones applied narrowly.
7.why: Cloudflare runs 0.2s on 147 elements; Gemini runs 0.2s on 74 and 0.3s on 54. The consistency is what reads as craft. A page with six durations on twenty elements reads as unfinished even when every individual choice is defensible.

8.rule: Two bands only: 0.1-0.16s for anything under the finger, 0.2-0.3s for anything that moves on its own. Nothing in between.
8.why: Every one of the four references separates these cleanly, and none of them uses a mid-range duration for a hover state.

9.rule: Fade an expensive layer IN after it is ready; never let first paint depend on it.
9.why: Cloudflare declares a canvas-fade-in keyframe for exactly this. Our own hero shipped a canvas that never ran at all, and because the CSS atmosphere underneath it was independent, the page still rendered a composition instead of a blank panel.

10.rule: A long page whose every section shows the product working beats a short page with an effect on top of it.
10.why: Gemini carries 29 videos and 10 keyframes. It is the least animated page of the five by authored motion and among the most alive to look at, because the motion is the product rather than the decoration.

screens.label: Code redemption — the one-field screen: where it hides, the text box, the confirm button, and what the game says back
demonstrates: the whole screen is five instances and no more: a Frame named 'Background' holding a Title TextLabel, a Description TextLabel, one TextBox and one TextButton, plus a UICorner — a codes screen that grows a sixth element has stopped being a codes screen

the opener is a SEPARATE TextButton ('CodesButton') living on the HUD, outside the panel, and it TOGGLES the panel rather than opening it: `background.Visible = not background.Visible`, so the same button closes it again
there is a line of instruction text between the title and the field — the field is not left to explain itself
sizes are authored in Scale with Offset pinned at zero ('0.1, 0, 0.1, 0', and the reader is told 'don't edit the 2nd and 4th values'), so the panel rescales rather than staying a fixed pixel box
three distinct replies, not two: 'Valid code', 'Already redeemed', 'Incorrect code' — 'already redeemed' is broken out from 'incorrect' at the very first tutorial level
codes are one-time-use PER PLAYER, checked against a per-player folder, so the already-redeemed reply is a normal outcome and not an error

the single most transferable construction decision in this whole file: the RESULT IS WRITTEN INTO THE FIELD'S OWN PlaceholderText, not into a separate status label — the TextBox clears on submit and its placeholder becomes the answer, so the player's eye never has to move off the box it was already on
the placeholder is recoloured per outcome: success green (Color3 0.333333, 1, 0.498039), failure red (Color3 1, 0.313725, 0.313725), resting grey (Color3 0.698039, 0.698039, 0.698039)
exact strings used: resting 'Type Here', success 'Code Redeemed', failure 'Invalid Code', third state 'Code Already Redeemed' — all title case, two or three words, no punctuation, no apology

the recoloured message is TRANSIENT: it displays for a beat and then resets to the default grey placeholder, so the screen returns to a resting state ready for the next code instead of holding an accusation on screen
the panel carries the player's currency readouts (Coins, Gems) live inside it, so the reward lands visibly in the same frame the player is looking at
three separate sounds are wired: a button click, an error sound for invalid/already-redeemed, and a distinct redeem sound for success — the audio carries the same three-way split as the colour
the panel has BOTH a close button of its own and the external toggle button; either dismisses it

the critique that repeats three times in one thread is about the close control, not the layout: 'make the X more thick so that it is more visible', 'make the X to close the UI a little bit thicker', 'the X is kinda small' — on a one-field modal the X is the second most-used control and gets built too small by default

'add a border to the "Redeem" button, so It will cover up the distortion against the background' — the confirm button needs its own stroke, because a green fill sitting directly on a coloured panel has no edge
'make everything bigger (buttons and text)' — a codes panel authored at desktop-cursor scale is too small the moment it is touched
'blur it a little bit, so the text is more visible' — the world behind the modal is blurred or dimmed rather than left sharp

a replier draws the genre line explicitly: a flat minimal treatment is 'too simple' for a cartoony game and 'simple is better for more realistic games and horror games' — the codes screen inherits the game's construction language, it does not have one of its own
the panel is built as a frame inside a frame: an outermost coloured border frame with a grey body frame inset within it, rather than a single frame carrying a UIStroke

the concrete geometry rule for that construction: 'The cornering on the outermost blue border does not go with the cornering of the gray background' — the fix given is to measure the gap between the two frames and ADD it to the inner radius to get the outer radius, otherwise the two curves diverge at the corners

'The text in the TextBox and "Redeem" button are noticeable closer to the top in each box' — centred text rides high in several Roblox fonts and needs a UIPadding correction; a codes screen is two boxes of centred text, so the defect shows twice
the same two elements are named as the whole screen again: the TextBox and the Redeem button

the codes UI is NOT a panel here: it is a SECTION inside the settings menu — 'Tap the Settings button (the cog) in the top-left corner', then 'Scroll down the settings menu until you see the "Redeem Codes" section'
in that inline form the field and the button share one ROW: the field on the left, 'the green Claim button on the right'
the placeholder is a lowercase invitation with an ellipsis: 'Type code here…' — not a label, not all-caps, and it sits inside the field
the confirm word is 'Claim', not 'Redeem' — the verb varies by game while the colour (green) does not
the codes affordance is reached in two taps from the HUD, and the HUD icon it hides behind is a gear in the top-left corner
the codes entry point is buried inside the SHOP, at the very bottom of it: open the store from the shopping cart icon, scroll to the bottom, and find 'a banner with a Redeem button in the corner'
so the affordance is a full-width BANNER row with the action button tucked into its corner — the same band construction the shop uses for a featured offer, reused for codes
tapping that banner's Redeem opens the actual entry surface, where the code is typed 'into the box' — two stages: an advertisement row, then the field
the confirm control is described by size and colour before it is described by label: 'the big green "Redeem!" button' — big, green, exclamation mark
the word 'Redeem' is used for BOTH the banner's opener and the confirm inside; the repetition is the shipped behaviour
the opener is a standalone HUD icon with no menu around it: 'Click the Present icon near the compass' — one tap from play to the field
the icon is a GIFT/PRESENT, and it is placed next to an unrelated HUD element (the compass) rather than in a tidy rail — codes affordances colonise whatever HUD corner is free
the confirm control is labelled 'Redeem'
this game previously used the Twitter-bird icon for the same job; the bird has been replaced by a present, so a generator that hard-codes a bird is reproducing a retired convention
the opener is a generic overflow button — 'the "Extra" button in the top-left corner' — and Codes is one item inside it, alongside whatever else did not earn its own HUD slot
the confirm control carries NO WORD AT ALL: 'Click the green check mark' — an icon-only green tick sitting beside the field
that is the floor of the convention: the confirm may lose its label, but it does not lose its green
codes is a SUB-SCREEN of an unrelated screen: 'Click the Profile button' on the right side of the screen, then 'Click the Codes button' in the top-left corner of the profile screen
