rules.note: Distilled from the references above. This is a SCREEN, not a genre: stroke weight, corner radius, bevel and text stroke come from the genre file the leaderboard is being built in (simulator.json for a cartoony game). What is here is the leaderboard's own construction — which surface it lives on, what a row is made of, how the top three differ, how scope and time window are expressed, and what the states are. Numbers are quoted from the sources named in each rule's `why`, not sampled from pixels.

surface.primary: a board standing in the world, on a SurfaceGui attached to a part, placed at or beside the spawn/lobby landmark
surface.secondary: a screen list, which is the SERVER list and a different thing from the global board
surface.never: a centred modal over the game — no fetched source puts a global leaderboard in one
surface.why: TDS flanks the elevators, Super Bomb Survival sits right of the teleport area, CONTROL sits 'directly in front of the spawning point', Infinite Tower Tycoon puts four on the centre spawn pad, Bee Swarm has 18 around the map, and the GLeaderboard module's constructor takes a Part. Five independent games and a published module agree, so the world board is the convention and the modal is the invention.

boardSet.rule: one board renders ONE stat over ONE window; more stats and more windows mean more boards, placed as a set
boardSet.arrangement: symmetrical — a flanking pair around a landmark, or a ring on the spawn pad
boardSet.overflow: past roughly four boards, the remainder move into a menu page and only the headline boards stay in the world
boardSet.why: TDS 'two boards ... on the sides of the Elevators', Super Bomb Survival's daily+global pair, CONTROL's two, Infinite Tower Tycoon's four on the pad, and Bee Swarm's split — '18 are able to be viewed at various locations around the map, and the rest are available to view in the System Page'

timeWindow.rule: the time window (daily / monthly / all-time) belongs in the board's TITLE and is fixed for that board — it is not a tab
timeWindow.signal: give the paired boards different frame colours so the window is readable before the title is
timeWindow.pairing: the same stat over two windows ships as two boards facing or flanking each other
timeWindow.resetDisclosure: a resetting board states its reset as a wall-clock time with a zone
timeWindow.why: Super Bomb Survival's 'Daily Leaderboard, which is indicated by the yellow-colored frame' beside the grey-framed Global one; Bee Swarm ships Daily / Monthly / All-Time Top Honeymakers as three separate boards and the all-time one sits 'on the opposite side of the path ... from the Daily Top Honeymakers leaderboard'; resets stated as '4:00 AM (UTC +0)' and '12:00am GMT-5'. A daily/all-time TAB was searched for and not found in any shipped game read here.

scopeSwitch.rule: the axis that IS switched in place is WHO, not WHEN: server / friends / global, as three views of one list
scopeSwitch.perViewLoading: each view is a separate fetch and needs its own loading and empty state
scopeSwitch.reserveGeometry: the switch's geometry is fixed by the control, never derived from its contents
scopeSwitch.why: the platform's own leaderboard is exactly this — 'Here, Friends, and Global are views of that same list' — and the beta thread reports 'a lag spike when swapping between here/friends/global' plus tabs that go 'squished when no score is configured'. A game that wants both axes should switch scope in the UI and split the window across boards.

row.order: left to right, exactly that order
row.minimumViable: rank, name, value — three text fields
row.aspect: ≈11.8 : 1 (width : height); about 16 rows to a full-height list
row.columnSplit: name ≈67% of the row, each numeric stat ≈17%
row.leftInset: ≈4% of row width, as proportional padding, not a pixel offset
row.cornerRadius: 2px — a row is a strip in a stack and does NOT take the card radius the rest of the game uses
row.pressable: a row is a control: it opens the person, and it must release camera input when it does
row.why: TDS names the fields in order — 'avatar icon, username, level and total statistic ... next to their spot'; the Roact rebuild gives the numbers — PlayerChip at UDim2.fromScale(0.99, 0.061) with aspect 11.76, name 67%, two stats at 17.1% each, 4% left padding, UDim.new(0, 2) radius; the tutorial's template has exactly Rank/Name/Value; and the new-leaderboard thread reports 'you cannot move your camera after pressing on someones name'

sectionHeaderRow.rule: a grouping row (team, bracket, section) is THINNER than a player row, not thicker
sectionHeaderRow.why: TeamChip is UDim2.fromScale(0.99, 0.046) at aspect 15.474 against the player row's 11.76 — the group bar reads as a divider, and a generator's instinct to make headers bigger inverts the hierarchy

avatar.shape: square, always — every thumbnail the engine serves is 1:1
avatar.rowFraming: HeadShot, requested one step above the slot's rendered size (48x48 for a ~40px slot)
avatar.podiumFraming: AvatarThumbnail (full body) for a podium figure, or a live posed character; never a HeadShot blown up
avatar.fetch: client-side, per row, and the row must render with a placeholder before it arrives
avatar.why: Enum.ThumbnailSize has exactly seven square values and ThumbnailType has exactly three framings — HeadShot 'head and up', AvatarBust 'chest up', AvatarThumbnail 'the entire body'. The published system renders the top three as full characters: 'The first three stand on the podium wearing their real Roblox avatar, playing a looping emote.'

podium.rule: the top three are a SEPARATE ASSEMBLY BESIDE OR ABOVE THE LIST, and they are ALSO still rows 1-3 in the list — the podium duplicates them, it does not remove them
podium.figure: a full-body avatar (or a live posed character), not the row's headshot
podium.why: TDS: 'Top three players are displayed on podiums next to the Leaderboards', while the same boards still list up to 50 players; the published system's headline is 'Top-3 Avatars' as a feature distinct from the board's rows
podium.notObserved: no fetched source states the left-to-right order or the relative heights of 1st/2nd/3rd. The familiar centre-highest arrangement was NOT confirmed in any source read here, so a generator should treat the ordering as a choice it is making, not a convention it is following. Searched: TDS wiki, the Leaderboard+Podium open-source thread (no layout stated), the Improving Podium System feedback thread (the only critique in it is about sound volume).

topThreeMarking.element: the ROW BACKGROUND colour, decided at row-clone time inside the loop where the rank is in scope
topThreeMarking.bands: exactly four — gold #1, silver #2, bronze #3, one neutral for every other rank
topThreeMarking.never: a gradient fading down the list, and never a colour on the rank glyph alone
topThreeMarking.why: the accepted answer in the rank-colour thread is 'when you clone the frame, check if the player's rank is for example 1 and if yes, change the BackgroundColor'; no shared RGBs exist in any source, so what is conventional is the element and the band count, not the hues

rankBadgeOutsideTheBoard.rule: a ranked player carries their standing out of the board and onto their character, and the badge carries the NUMBER
rankBadgeOutsideTheBoard.iconIdentifiesBoard: a different icon per board (crown for the daily board, star for the wins board), and boards without a reward tier get no icon
rankBadgeOutsideTheBoard.standingDepth: the badge can be granted far deeper than the board renders
rankBadgeOutsideTheBoard.why: Super Bomb Survival: 'A ranked player will have special icons with a number corresponding to their ranking position above them', crown for the daily top 10 and star for Top 10 Wins, and after v3.30.4 'players within the top 100 will also have special icons above them. Though, they are still not listed on the boards.' TDS grants the top three a Champion Nametag they keep after the month ends.

depth.paging: vertical scroll inside the board, not arrow pagination
depth.why: Bee Swarm states it exactly — 'displays the ranks of the top 100 players, showing ten ranks at a time' and 'The player can scroll down the leaderboard to see more players, all the way to the 100th place'; Super Bomb Survival shows 10; GLeaderboard's example passes 10; TDS goes to 50; the tutorial fetches TotalEntires = 50 in pages of 5. Ten visible is unanimous across four independent sources.

listContainer.rule: a ScrollingFrame with AutomaticCanvasSize = Y and a UIListLayout; CanvasSize authored at zero
listContainer.rowPlacement: LayoutOrder = rank; never compute a Position per row
listContainer.rowLifecycle: rows are cloned from one template, keyed by rank, and DIFFED on refresh — a rank whose occupant has not changed is left untouched
listContainer.why: the tutorial: 'new.LayoutOrder = Rank', 'AutomaticCanvasSize is set to Y', CanvasSize {0,0},{0,0}; the published system: 'A rank whose player has not changed is left alone, so only a real change costs a lookup'. A hardcoded CanvasSize is the standard defect this avoids, and diffing is what makes a rank change the one place an animation belongs.

valueColumn.alignment: right, in a FIXED width reserved before any data arrives
valueColumn.widthSource: size it from the widest value the board can hold, never from the first row
valueColumn.format: one of three, chosen per board: raw, comma-separated, or abbreviated to ≤4 significant digits plus a magnitude suffix
valueColumn.abbreviateWhen: the board's values can exceed roughly six digits
valueColumn.truncation: never — a clipped number shows its least significant digits, which is worse than showing nothing
valueColumn.why: the published system offers exactly 52500 / 52,500 / 52.5K per board; Bee Swarm's Onett 'abbreviated the amount of honey ... due to players having massive amounts of honey' and its top ten reads 1.6219 Qn down to 1.0002 Qn — near-identical widths and only 1.6x between first and tenth, so the column must not be sized from the leader; CONTROL's board carries 10,137,426 at full length; and the beta thread reports a value column 'showing the tail end of the number'

nameColumn.rule: the name is the ONLY flexible column — rank, avatar and value are fixed, and the name absorbs the remainder
nameColumn.truncation: truncate at the END with an ellipsis; never let the start be clipped
nameColumn.nameKind: display name, with username as an explicit authored toggle
nameColumn.composite: if the game prefixes a rank title, the name cell is a two-part composite and needs more room than a username
nameColumn.why: Bee Swarm's real top ten runs from 'ruiream' to 'roblox_user_494351377' in one column; the beta thread reports 'names are being cropped out'; the platform list sorts and shows 'Display Names'; CONTROL renders 'Commissioner X aestheticminerald' — title then name, inline

badgeSlot.rule: reserve a slot between the avatar and the name for role/entitlement icons — developer, admin, premium, gamepass holder
badgeSlot.why: the platform player list has carried this slot through every redesign, its contents replaced each time (Builders Club hard hats, then Premium, then the game-owner ribbon 'a white hammer with a coding symbol (<>)', the administrator tilted-O, the Video Stars shooting star), and the Leaderboard+ plugin exposes it as an authorable feature: 'custom symbols for admins, premium users, and gamepass holders'

sorting.rule: descending on the FIRST column; the first column IS the sort key, so column order must be authored explicitly
sorting.mechanism: IsPrimary (a child BoolValue) beats Priority (a child NumberValue, higher first, default 0), which beats insertion order
sorting.fallback: with no leaderboard at all, the server list sorts alphabetically by display name
sorting.why: the Roblox Wiki states the platform rule outright — sorted 'from the highest value of the leaderboard's first column to the lowest value of the same column' — and the docs give the three ordering mechanisms with 'IsPrimary takes precedence over any Priority values'

ownStanding.observedForm: a SEPARATE readout outside the ranked list — a proximity message at the board, or a value shown in a menu — written as a full sentence naming the stat, because outside the list there is no column header to read the number against
ownStanding.notObserved: a pinned own-rank row inside or beneath the list was searched for and NOT found in any source read here. Searched: the platform leaderboards doc, the persistent-leaderboards beta thread and its replies, four shipped-game wikis (Bee Swarm, Super Bomb Survival, TDS, Infinite Tower Tycoon), the global-leaderboard tutorial, GLeaderboard, Leaderboard+, and two DevForum feedback threads. A generator may still build one, but it should know it is inventing, not citing.
ownStanding.why: Bee Swarm: 'Upon standing on the white pad in front of a leaderboard, it will show a message stating the player's score for the corresponding leaderboard', and the Top Brown Bear Helpers board — the one that shows no value column — pushes the player's own score into the menu or an NPC instead

refresh.disclose: show the board's staleness — a next-refresh countdown, or a stated note that updates lag
refresh.why: the tutorial's 'RefreshTime = 15 -- In Seconds'; GLeaderboard's example UPDATE_TIME of 60; the published system 'refresh on an interval you set' with next-refresh timing displayed; Bee Swarm 'usually not in real-time but update very often'; Infinite Tower Tycoon prints 'Note: There is a delay between updates' on the board

screenListPlacement.rule: if a leaderboard is drawn on screen, either disable the platform one or stay out of the top-right corner
screenListPlacement.sizeToOccupancy: the screen list's height is computed from the number of players present, not fixed
screenListPlacement.why: the docs give SetCoreGuiEnabled as the documented way to hide it; developers complained the platform list 'was covering my game UI', 'covers f3x uis', obscures 'the networkping from performance stats', and is 'wasting my screen space ... even tho im the only person in the server' with the request to shrink it when alone. The same critique was made of a custom board — 'when there's one player in a team, it's as big as if there were more players'.

serverListVsGlobalBoard.rule: they are different objects with different contents, and players name them differently
serverListVsGlobalBoard.serverList: text-only rows, no avatars, sorted by the first stat, rebuilt as players join and leave
serverListVsGlobalBoard.globalBoard: avatars, podium, rank badges, persisted, refreshed on an interval
serverListVsGlobalBoard.why: the Infinite Tower Tycoon wiki opens by disambiguating them — 'Not too be confused with the UI Leaderboard on the top right corner of the screen'; the Leaderboard+ in-screen plugin offers no thumbnails at all while every in-world global board carries them

states.loading: render the row skeleton with the rank numbers already in place — ranks are known before names are
states.empty: the columns keep their widths; an unconfigured or empty board must not collapse its tab row or its value column
states.playerLeaves: a server-list row keyed to a player is DESTROYED on PlayerRemoving
states.removedEntry: a moderated-out entry disappears and the ranks below close up — there is no struck-through or flagged state
states.why: the beta thread's 'squished when no score is configured'; Leaderboard+'s public defect 'whenever a player leaves the leaderboard stays on'; Bee Swarm's 'Only legitimate players appear on the leaderboards for lengths of time (exploiters will be removed)'

rewardBrackets.rule: if a board pays out, the payout is banded by rank and the bands are far deeper than the ten rows on screen
rewardBrackets.why: TDS grants the top three of either board a Champion Nametag; Super Bomb Survival grants icons to the top 100 who are 'still not listed on the boards'; Pet Simulator 99's Time Trials leaderboards pay out in exactly those brackets. The bands are attested in the DATA; none of the fetched sources describes how (or whether) a bracket threshold is drawn on the board itself, so this rule tells a generator the bands exist and does NOT tell it they are rendered as separators.

categoryControl.rule: when one board must cover several related stats, the category control sits at the TOP of the board as arrows and the rows scroll vertically beneath it — or the board rotates categories on its own with no control at all
categoryControl.why: Infinite Tower Tycoon's Board 2 'is scrollable using the arrows on top' across Kills/Crates/Keys/Codes; Super Bomb Survival's global board 'cycles through multiple categories' unattended. Two shipped answers, neither of which is a tab row.

themePerBoard.rule: boards in the same game are allowed to look different from each other; the row template is shared, the chrome is not
themePerBoard.why: the published system states it as a selling point — 'A cash board and a wins board can look nothing alike' — and ships three board templates each with its own podium styling; GLeaderboard exposes exactly TopBar, TopLine, Title, TitleStroke and ScrollBar as the restyleable parts, all chrome

screens.label: The BATTLE PASS / SEASON PASS screen, across genres — the tier track, the free and premium lanes, reward nodes and their four states, the season XP bar, the claim action, the premium upsell and its confirmation, the season timer, the mission list that feeds the track, and the HUD opener that badges it
demonstrates: The screen is a WIDE, SHORT landscape band — roughly 2:1 — not a tall modal. A ten-tier track has to run across the screen, so the pass panel is the widest and shortest panel a game owns.

The tier track is a single thick BLACK horizontal bar running edge to edge inside the panel, with ten small rounded-square number badges sitting ON the bar at even spacing. The bar is the spine; the badges are the only thing on it.
Tier numbers are gold rounded squares with a heavy dark stroke, set in the same display face as the titles — the number is a badge, not plain text on a line.

Free rewards sit ABOVE the bar, premium rewards BELOW it, and each reward tile is joined to its tier badge by a short thin vertical LEADER LINE. The tile does not sit in a cell; it hangs off the spine.
The two lanes are OFFSET by half a step: free tiles land on even tiers, premium tiles on odd tiers, so the columns interleave instead of stacking. Nothing forces the lanes to share a column.

The premium lane is identified by a full-width coloured BAND behind it whose left end carries the lane label in two short lines; the free lane has no band at all. Band presence, not tile colour, is what separates the lanes.
Every reward tile carries a small CIRCULAR category badge overhanging its top-right corner — what kind of thing the reward is (vehicle, texture, effect) is a second glyph on the tile, not a word.
Free tiles are dark rounded squares; premium tiles are light rounded squares on the band. The tile fill flips between lanes so the tile stays legible against whatever is behind it.

The header is a full-width band across the panel top, split by a DIAGONAL cut: the left zone holds the season number in a gold outlined display face, the season name beside it in a contrasting weight, and a small all-caps instruction line beneath; the right zone holds the timer. The split is a slanted edge, not a rule or a gap.
The timer block is two lines: a small all-caps label over a large coloured figure, and it reads in coarse units (days and hours) rather than seconds until it is nearly out.

The footer is two wide buttons side by side. The left one is the upsell: a pill with a small pass icon at its left, a small italic eyebrow line naming the season above the label, the buy label large, and the price as a number followed by the hard-currency glyph. The right one is the sibling action into the mission list, or its disabled stand-in when the season has ended.
The close control is a small circle at the TOP-LEFT corner, overhanging the panel — the pass screen is the one screen that does not put close at the top-right.
A separate strip sits below the panel entirely for gifting: label, a small square avatar box, a dark text field with placeholder, and a purchase pill at the right.

When the season has ended the timer reads zero, the right footer button becomes a flat disabled block with a waiting label, and the header subtitle is swapped for a thanks-and-next-season line. The track itself is left on screen unchanged.

ANNOTATION, NOT UI: in -4 through -8 the publisher dims the whole capture and draws a light-blue-plus-violet double outline around whichever element the surrounding text is discussing. That double outline is not part of the game's UI and must not be copied as a selection style.
Same skeleton in a completely different visual register: dark, flat, no strokes, no bevels, no text outline. The battle-pass SHAPE is genre-independent; only the surface changes.
Two lanes of reward CARDS with a horizontal tier rail running BETWEEN them, and here the lanes are column-ALIGNED: tier N is the same x in both lanes.

A fixed left gutter column, about a seventh of the width, holds the lane identity: a small pass/ticket glyph with the lane name beneath it, vertically centred to its lane. The gutter does not scroll with the track.
The lanes are distinguished by CARD TINT, not by a band: free cards are neutral dark, premium cards a tinted dark of the same value. No divider, no label band.
The tier rail IS the progress bar. The completed run of the rail is a thick bright line; the remaining run is a thin dim line; the break between them sits at the player's current tier.
Tier chips are small flag/hexagon pills sitting ON the rail at each column boundary. Reached chips are filled light with dark text; unreached chips are dark with dim text. Same shape, inverted fill.
Card slot order is fixed: art in the top ~60%, the reward NAME in bold beneath it, then a state slot pinned at the bottom. The name never changes between states.

Four states live in that one bottom slot: claimable renders a filled accent button spanning the card's inner width; claimed renders a bare tick glyph and nothing else; unreached renders NOTHING, leaving the slot empty; premium-locked renders a padlock glyph followed by one muted word. The card is otherwise identical in all four.
Locked and unreached reward ART is drawn at full colour and full opacity. Nothing is greyed out; the state is carried entirely by the bottom slot.

The top bar is one black band: season number large at the left with the season name and the remaining time on ONE small muted line beneath it, separated by a middle dot; the tab row centred; the progress readout and close at the right.

The progress readout at the top right is a compact cluster: a small tier chip, then the XP fraction as current-over-target, then a thin rounded bar directly underneath showing that fraction filled. It is a readout, not the main track.
Tabs are plain text labels, active one bright and inactive one dim, each with a small coloured DOT to its right when that tab has something to collect. The dot is the badge.

The upsell button sits at the BOTTOM-LEFT, directly under the premium lane's gutter label, as a quiet dark rounded button with a ticket glyph, the buy label, and the price as a currency glyph then a number.
Horizontal scroll is signalled by CLIPPING: the rightmost column is cut by the panel edge mid-card rather than ending flush. A flush right edge would read as the end of the track.
Close is a bare X glyph with no button behind it — in a flat register the close chrome disappears entirely.

The HUD opener sits at the screen's right edge outside the panel: a circular art button with a small coloured badge dot at its top-right, and two caption lines beneath giving the season name and the remaining time.

The screen has three fixed regions and one scrolling one: a left INFO RAIL, a lane-label column, the scrolling tier grid, and the season XP bar between the lanes. The callout states explicitly that the info rail stays anchored while the player scrolls the tiers.

The info rail, about a sixth of the width, stacks: season title, a small time-remaining line in days/hours/minutes, a short instruction sentence, and lower down the upgrade button with the premium glyph and a one-line reason to press it.

The lane-label column is the first column of the grid, not part of the rail: a header cell reading the word tiers, then a free-lane cell and a premium-lane cell, each an icon above a two-line lane name.
Column headers are the bare tier NUMBERS in a header row above the free lane. The number is a column heading, not a chip inside the cell.

The season XP bar is a full-width strip BETWEEN the two lanes, labelled at its left end, with a small XP pennant marker. It fills left to right and the edge of the fill lands under the tier the player is on — the bar and the grid share one x-axis.
A reward cell is: icon, quantity beneath as a times-n line, then a state slot at the bottom of the cell. Every cell is the same rectangle.

The state slot matrix, stated as such across five successive wireframes: unreached = empty slot; reached-and-unclaimed = a bordered claim button; claimed = the button is REMOVED and replaced by the bare past-tense word, no box; premium-not-owned = a padlock glyph, with the premium ROW additionally carrying a different background tint from the free row.

The callout is explicit that the claimed state removes the button rather than disabling it, and that the lock means the reward cannot be claimed until the pass is bought — the lock is about ownership, not about progress.

Buying the pass changes four things at once: every padlock disappears, every already-completed premium tier immediately shows an enabled claim button, the rail's upgrade button is removed and replaced by a plain unlocked line, and the mission panel's upgrade button becomes a non-interactive upgraded label.

rules.note: Distilled from the ten references above. Units are Roblox UI units: px for stroke and radius, screen fractions for panel size, unitless for scale. Proportions were read off screenshots and wireframes by eye and are stated as approximations. Where the references disagree, the rule says which way the majority goes and what the minority case is for. Colour is deliberately absent: the same skeleton appears in a saturated cartoon register and in a flat dark one, so colour is not what makes this screen read as a battle pass.

panelShape.aspect: 2.0-2.6 wide to tall for the track screen
panelShape.why: every track reference is a wide short band, because ten columns have to fit across; the single most common way a generated pass screen goes wrong is inheriting the shop's tall portrait modal and then stacking the tiers vertically to make them fit

order: header or top bar (season identity + timer + progress readout + close)
lane gutter or lane label column (fixed, does not scroll)
footer (upsell at the left, sibling action at the right)
regions.scrolls: the two lanes and the rail scroll together on one shared x-axis; the gutter, header and footer are pinned
regions.why: four of the references separate exactly these regions and one of them names them as fixed frames; a pass whose lane labels scroll away with the track loses which row is which as soon as the player moves

trackOrientation.default: horizontal, two lanes stacked, one column per tier
trackOrientation.minority: vertical only when the tier count is large enough that a horizontal track would need many pages; none of the references did this
trackOrientation.never: a single merged lane with free and premium interleaved in one row
trackOrientation.why: unanimous across every reference including the two official wireframe decks; the free-above/premium-below stack is the thing that makes the screen recognisable at a glance

laneOrder.rule: free lane ABOVE, premium lane BELOW, always
laneOrder.why: all six references that show both lanes put free on top; the order carries the upsell — the player reads what they get, then what they are missing

mustCarryAtLeastOneOf: a fixed gutter cell at the left with an icon above a short lane name
a full-width coloured band behind the premium lane whose left end carries the label
a full-width label band between the two lanes
a different card tint for the premium lane
laneIdentity.why: each reference picks a different one of these four and every reference picks at least one; a generator that relies on 'the bottom row is premium' produces a screen nobody can read cold

laneAlignment.aligned: tier N is the same x in both lanes — the default, and what a grid layout gives you free
laneAlignment.offset: free rewards on even tiers and premium on odd, so the lanes interleave; used when rewards are sparse and a cell-for-cell grid would be mostly empty
laneAlignment.why: the shipped racing-game pass offsets the lanes precisely because not every tier grants both; the flat package aligns them because every tier grants both. Sparseness decides, not taste

tierRail.rule: the rail between the lanes IS the season progress bar; do not draw a separate season bar elsewhere in the body
tierRail.geometry: full width of the track area, 6-10% of the panel height, running edge to edge under the free lane
tierRail.fill: the completed run is thicker and brighter; the remaining run is thinner and dimmer; the break sits under the player's current tier
tierRail.why: three independent references put the progress on the rail rather than beside it, which is what ties the number 'tier 6' to a position on screen; a pass with a progress bar in the header and an inert track makes the player do the mapping themselves

tierNode.shape: a small badge sitting ON the rail — rounded square, hexagon or flag pill
tierNode.content: the tier number and nothing else
tierNode.sizeRelativeToRail: 1.4-1.8x the rail thickness, so the badge sits proud of the line
tierNode.reachedVsUnreached: same shape, inverted fill — reached is filled with dark text, unreached is dark or outlined with dim text
tierNode.never: a plain number floating beside the line with no badge
tierNode.why: four references badge the number and invert the fill on reach; inverting the fill is what makes the boundary between reached and unreached legible without reading a single digit

tierCount.range: 10 for a month-long season; more only if the track pages or scrolls
tierCount.why: both official documents name ten as the starting point and both wireframe decks draw exactly ten; the two shipped games in the references both ship ten

overflow.preferred: horizontal scroll, with the rightmost column CLIPPED mid-card by the panel edge so the cut signals more content
overflow.alternative: pagination — a row of small circular numbered page buttons at the top-right, active one filled
overflow.scrollbarRole: an indicator that scrolling exists; dragging anywhere in the track must also scroll it
overflow.autoScroll: on open, scroll to the first UNCLAIMED reward rather than to tier 1 or to the current tier
overflow.why: the wireframe deck states the indicator role and the auto-scroll rule in its own callouts; the clipped-column cue appears in three references and a flush right edge reads as the end of the track

slotOrder: rewardName (optional — dropped when the art is self-explanatory)
rewardCell.stateSlotHeight: ~18-22% of the cell height, pinned to the bottom padding
rewardCell.categoryBadge: an optional small circular glyph overhanging the cell's top-right corner, naming the KIND of reward
rewardCell.why: every reference stacks art, then identity, then state, in that order and with the state against the bottom edge; the state slot is the same rectangle in every state, which is what stops the grid jumping as rewards are claimed

fourStates.rule: all four reward states change ONE slot at the bottom of the cell and change nothing else
fourStates.unreached: the slot is EMPTY — the absence is the state
fourStates.claimable: a filled button spanning the cell's inner width, one short verb
fourStates.claimed: the button is REMOVED and replaced by the bare past-tense word or a single tick glyph — no box, no outline, no disabled button
fourStates.premiumLocked: a padlock glyph, optionally followed by one muted word naming the track
fourStates.artNeverChanges: reward art stays at full colour and full opacity in all four states
fourStates.why: this matrix is stated explicitly in the official wireframe deck and rendered identically by the shipped package; greying the art is the most common wrong answer and it destroys the thing the upsell is selling — the player has to be able to SEE what they are locked out of

lockIsOwnershipNotProgress.rule: the padlock means the premium pass is not owned. It never means the tier is not yet reached
lockIsOwnershipNotProgress.corollary: an unreached FREE reward shows nothing at all; an unreached PREMIUM reward shows the padlock, because both facts are true and ownership is the one the screen is selling
lockIsOwnershipNotProgress.why: the wireframe callouts distinguish the two and the package ships them as different slot contents; a generator that locks everything ahead of the player collapses the upsell into ordinary progression

claimIsExplicit.rule: rewards are claimed by pressing a button, never auto-granted on tier-up
claimIsExplicit.consequence: the screen must be able to show many claimable cells at once, and the HUD opener must badge when any exist
claimIsExplicit.endOfSeason: if the season ends with anything unclaimed, deliver it in a modal — a headline, a one-line explanation, an inner bordered box holding the outstanding reward icons with quantities, and ONE claim button under them
claimIsExplicit.why: stated as best practice in the official design document with its reasoning (an automatic grant goes unnoticed, and a claim drives a return visit) and drawn as its own wireframe state

finalTier.rule: the last tier's cell is emphasised and is the ONLY cell whose weight differs
finalTier.how: a much heavier border, or a larger cell, carrying a label rather than an icon-and-quantity
finalTier.tapOpens: an info popup — large square art block at the LEFT, and at the right the item name, a one-line requirement sentence, flavour text, and any stats
finalTier.why: both wireframe decks draw the final cell at heavier weight and give it its own popup; the shipped racing pass ends its track on an oversized reward too. The capstone is the reason the player finishes the season and a track that ends on an ordinary cell has no ending

seasonTimer.placement: top-right of the header, or on its own line directly under the season name
seasonTimer.format: coarse units, largest two only — days and hours, dropping to hours and minutes near the end; never a bare seconds count while days remain
seasonTimer.label: a small all-caps label above or beside the figure, never the figure alone
seasonTimer.why: every reference shows the timer and three of them repeat it in the upsell path; the wireframe deck states outright that putting the countdown in the purchase dialog is deliberate

progressReadouts.rule: the screen carries TWO progress figures at different scales and they are different frames
progressReadouts.currentTier: a compact cluster at the top right — a small tier chip, the XP fraction as current-over-target, and a thin bar directly beneath showing that fraction
progressReadouts.wholeSeason: the tier rail itself, filling through the tier badges
progressReadouts.why: Roblox's own package separates a tier-progress frame from a season-progress frame; one bar cannot answer both 'how far into this tier' and 'how far through the season'

upsellPanel.placement: bottom-left of the screen, under the premium lane's label, or as the lower half of the left info rail
contents: the price as a number and the hard-currency glyph
an eyebrow or sub-line naming the season, or one line of reason
upsellPanel.shape: a wide pill or ticket — the ticket variant is notched on its vertical edges
upsellPanel.never: a bare price with no glyph, and never the only mention of the premium track on the screen
upsellPanel.why: five references put the buy control at the bottom-left or the rail's foot with exactly this content; the price-with-glyph rule is unanimous across the whole library

tierSkipOffer.rule: a tier-skip or bundle is a SECOND button beside the plain pass, never the same button
tierSkipOffer.marking: a best-value tag overhanging its top-left corner, and a separate darker sub-band beneath the label stating the number of tiers granted
tierSkipOffer.why: seen as a distinct tagged block in the community pass and called out by its reviewers; folding the skip into the pass button hides which of the two the player is buying

purchaseConfirmation.rule: the upsell opens a confirmation dialog before spending, it does not buy on press
contents: the premium glyph and the time-remaining line together at the top-left
a benefit headline plus a smaller line promising that completed tiers are claimable retroactively
the price as a number followed by the hard-currency glyph
confirm and cancel side by side
purchaseConfirmation.why: drawn as its own wireframe with callouts saying a confirmation is best practice whenever real money is spent and that the retroactive promise is what removes the penalty for waiting

afterPurchase.rule: buying the pass changes four things in one frame
changes: every already-completed premium tier immediately shows an enabled claim button
the upgrade button is REMOVED and replaced by a plain unlocked line — not disabled in place
any sibling upgrade control elsewhere becomes a non-interactive upgraded label
afterPurchase.why: three successive wireframes show exactly this transition; leaving a live upgrade button on a screen the player already upgraded is the defect the deck was drawn to prevent

slotOrder: difficulty or tier badge with its label
reward tile (art with the quantity at its corner)
missionRow.progressBar: either a thin full-width bar with the fraction set INSIDE or immediately left of it, or — for a short mission — a bare fraction line with no bar at all
missionRow.rewardIsATile: the reward is a tile or a filled pill; never bare text beside the button
missionRow.actionIsSeparate: the reward tile and the action control are two adjacent slots, not one combined button
missionRow.trackPin: an optional small pin glyph at the row's top-right, for surfacing that mission on the HUD
missionRow.why: three references and both wireframe decks agree on this order; the one variation is whether the bar exists, and that is decided by whether the objective has a count

missionRowStates.complete: bar fully filled and the action enabled
missionRowStates.claimed: the action control removed and replaced by the bare past-tense word
missionRowStates.locked: the whole row darkened toward the panel's darkest value, a lock or shield glyph centred over it, and ONE centred sentence stating what unlocks it
missionRowStates.premium: marked twice — a small badge on the category ICON and a padlock over the action — plus a different row fill from the free rows
missionRowStates.why: the locked-row treatment and the double marking of premium rows are both drawn with callouts; a locked row that is merely dimmed without the sentence leaves the player with no next step

missionCadenceTabs.rule: daily and weekly are tabs over the SAME row anatomy; what changes is the row FILL and the per-mission XP figure, not the layout
missionCadenceTabs.refreshTimer: right-aligned on the section-title line, gaining a days field for the weekly tab, same unit order
missionCadenceTabs.emptyState: when every available mission is done, replace the list area with a centred congratulations line and KEEP the tier-progress strip below it
missionCadenceTabs.why: the two Dragon Adventures captures are the same panel with a different row hue, and the wireframe deck draws the all-complete state as a list replacement that leaves the progress strip in place

missionPanelTierStrip.rule: the mission panel carries a miniature of the whole pass pinned to its bottom
missionPanelTierStrip.contents: XP glyph, the current tier label at the left and the next tier label at the right of a bar with the fraction inside it, the season-ends line beneath, and the upgrade control at the right
missionPanelTierStrip.why: drawn in both official wireframes and in the shipped package's own tab pair; it is the bridge that tells the player why the missions matter, and a mission list without it is a chore list

header.style: a full-width band across the panel top, not a floating plaque
header.split: when the header carries both identity and timer, separate them with a DIAGONAL cut or a chevron rather than a vertical rule
header.contents: season number or name large, the season's theme name beside it, a small all-caps instruction line beneath, and the timer in the right zone
header.tabs: when the screen has sibling tabs, they go centred in the header, active bright and inactive dim, each carrying a small dot badge when that tab has something to collect
header.why: the pass screen is too wide for the overhanging plaque the shop uses — four references run a full-width band instead, and two of them cut it diagonally

closeButton.rule: a circle or gem proud of a panel corner, as elsewhere in the library
closeButton.corner: top-right by default; the shipped racing pass puts it top-LEFT, which is a legitimate minority when the header's right zone is occupied by the timer
closeButton.flatRegister: in a flat dark register the chrome disappears entirely and close is a bare glyph
closeButton.why: the timer block competes for the top-right corner on this screen specifically, which is why this is the one screen where the corner is negotiable

hudOpener.rule: the opener lives in the ordinary HUD rail at the same tile size as its neighbours and is distinguished by CONTENT, not by size
contents: a caption plate with the season name or number
a second line giving the time remaining
a badge dot at the top-right when anything is claimable
hudOpener.why: two independent references put the countdown inside the button and both official documents call for badging it; an oversized special button breaks the rail's rhythm and still does not say how long is left

betweenSeasons.rule: when the season has ended, REPLACE the track rather than leaving an inert one on screen
betweenSeasons.contents: a teaser image block at the left and a next-season countdown at the right, or a coming-soon headline with the countdown beneath
betweenSeasons.shippedVariant: one shipped game instead leaves the track visible, zeroes the timer, swaps the subtitle for a thanks line and turns the sibling footer button into a disabled waiting block
betweenSeasons.why: the official deck draws the replacement and a shipped game draws the softer variant; the failure both avoid is a live-looking track with nothing claimable and a timer at zero

surfacingBeyondTheScreen.rule: the pass is expected to surface in three places besides its own screen
places: the badged HUD opener with the countdown in it
a mission row pinned to the HUD via the row's pin control
an in-world showcase of the final reward on a plinth under season signage
surfacingBeyondTheScreen.why: the official guidance lists these surfacing methods and a shipped game's own capture is of the in-world showcase rather than of any UI; a pass that exists only behind a menu button under-performs its own content

constructionNotColour.rule: the same skeleton must render in any theme — the references include a saturated cartoon pass, a stone-and-ribbon mission panel and a flat dark package screen, and all three are the same construction
constructionNotColour.whatCarriesTheGenre: stroke weight, corner radius, text stroke, bevel and header treatment, taken from the genre file
constructionNotColour.whatDoesNot: lane order, rail-as-progress, the four-state slot, the claim-not-grant rule, the final-tier emphasis, the timer's placement
constructionNotColour.why: this file exists because a correct palette on wrong construction still looks wrong; on this screen the reverse also holds, and the flat package screen proves it by being unmistakably a battle pass with no stroke, no bevel and no outline anywhere

screens.label: The DAILY REWARDS / login-streak screen, across genres — day strips and calendars, claimed vs claimable vs locked vs missed tiles, streak counters, countdown timers, the claim button and the HUD opener that badges it
demonstrates: A seven-day streak is NOT necessarily one row of seven: this one runs as a 4-across grid that wraps 4 + 3, with the seventh tile simply ending the second row and no filler in the empty cells.

There is no tile card at all — no fill, no stroke, no rounded rect. Each reward is art, then a bold name under it, then a state row under that. The grid reads from the rhythm of the art and the label rows, on a body that carries a faint dotted texture.
Claimable state is a filled chip under the name: a wide flat rounded bar the width of the label, with a horizontal gradient that is lighter in the middle, a thin outline, and the single word 'Ready'.

Locked state DELETES the chip rather than dimming it. Days 4-7 have no bar at all — just a small padlock glyph followed by grey text reading 'Day 4', 'Day 5', 'Day 6', 'Day 7'. The state's absence is the state.

Locked reward art is NOT greyed, dimmed or hidden. All four locked icons are drawn at full colour and full opacity, identical in treatment to the claimable ones; only the label row beneath them differs.
The reward NAME stays white and bold in every state — the name is never the thing that changes.

Claiming is one footer action, not per tile: a full-width footer band holds a centred sentence ('Play daily to unlock rewards!') and a single primary 'Claim Rewards' button pinned to the far right in a light accent blue, with a small corner radius relative to its height, not a pill.
The header is a full-width band across the panel top, inset inside the panel rather than overhanging it, with the title centred, a bare × glyph at the far right and a thin divider under it.

Tabs are plain text labels at the LEFT of that header band ('Time', 'Daily'), the active one white and the inactive grey, each with a small coloured dot to its right. The dot is a has-something-waiting badge, not the selection indicator — both tabs carry one.
Same screen, other tab, and the construction is identical — one grid component serves both a time-played ladder and a daily streak. The tab swaps the data and the footer sentence, nothing structural.

With every reward claimable at once, every tile carries its own 'Ready' chip and there is still exactly ONE claim button, in the footer. The per-tile chip reports state; the footer button performs the action.

A vertical scrollbar sits inside the right edge of the content area and a partial row is visibly clipped at the bottom — the reward grid scrolls under a fixed header and a fixed footer, rather than the panel growing.
Gutters are wide relative to the art: roughly a full icon's width between columns, so eight tiles fill a panel that is close to full-screen.
The footer sentence is the tab's own configured description line, sitting to the left of the claim button rather than above the grid.

The reward record that the UI renders has exactly four fields — icon (an image asset id, explicitly not a decal), displayName, quantity (defaulting to 1), and effect. A tile has four slots because the data has four fields.

Rarity is a SWAPPED BACKGROUND FRAME, not a colour tweak: marking a reward `effect = Types.RewardEffect.Valuable` 'give[s] it a different background frame in the UI', and adding a new effect means adding a whole frame to RewardItemFrames. Rarity and state therefore live in different layers and cannot collide.

The claimable look is named in the objects the docs tell you to restyle: 'FooterContentFrame.ClaimableUIGradient' — the claimable treatment is a gradient on a footer frame, which matches the gradient chips seen in the two screenshots.
A persistent HUD opener is part of the package, named 'RewardsHudButton.Background' — the rewards screen ships with its own on-screen button rather than relying on a generic menu.

The screen opens itself: `isHiddenOnJoin` defaults to false, meaning 'rewards automatically pop up when joining the game if the player has a new daily reward to claim'. Auto-open is conditional on something being claimable.

Two reset policies are offered and the difference is spelled out: `isAlignedToStreakResetTime` true means day 2 unlocks 24 hours after the day-1 claim; false means day 2 unlocks at the first midnight after it, so a player who claims at 23:00 can claim again an hour later. Day 3 onward is always 24 hours after the previous day's claimable time.
Tabs are data, not layout: `tabDisplayName` and `tabOrder` on each reward type, plus a per-tab `description` string that the footer renders.
Seven day tiles in a SINGLE ROW of equal width, on a panel roughly 60% of screen width and 38% of screen height — the strip is the panel's whole purpose and it is sized to hold seven across.
The tile is a TALL portrait card, roughly 1:2 width to height, radius small relative to its size (~8px), flat dark fill, no stroke in the default state.

Tile slot order, top to bottom, is fixed: 'DAY n' label, reward icon, amount text, state chip pinned to the bottom edge. Four slots, always in that order, and the chip always touches the bottom padding.

The claimable tile changes THREE things at once: its fill becomes the accent colour, it gains a lighter stroke the default tiles do not have, and it is scaled up about 6-8% so it breaks the row's top and bottom alignment. Its chip becomes a green 'CLAIM' button with a darker bottom edge.
Locked tiles keep their full-colour art and change only the chip, which becomes a flat grey rounded rect reading 'LOCKED' in dark small caps.

The final day is colour-promoted regardless of state: day 7 is gold with an amber stroke, and its amount text is replaced by the reward's NAME in two lines ('LEGENDARY PET') while it still carries the ordinary grey LOCKED chip. Rarity and state are independent channels on the same tile.
Under the strip sits a full-width progress track — a light pill with a dark outline — with the text '0 / 7 DAYS' centred INSIDE the track, over the fill rather than beside it.

The footer is two corner-anchored lines, not a centred one: the streak counter at the left ('0 DAY STREAK', the number and word in one green outlined string) and the status at the right ('REWARD READY!').
The header is a coloured band inset across the panel's top inner edge, title left-aligned in small all-caps with an × at the band's right end — a band, not an overhanging plaque.

The opener is a small vertical stack of icon buttons pinned to the LEFT screen edge at mid-height, each with its own live countdown text directly beneath the icon, and a red badge dot on the one with something waiting.

CLAIMED is the only state that touches the art. The claimed tile desaturates wholesale — fill goes to a pale neutral, the coin icon renders in muted grey-gold, the amount text goes grey — while locked tiles beside it keep full-colour art. Dimming means 'spent', never 'not yet'.
The claimed chip does not say 'CLAIMED'. It becomes a pale green rounded rect containing a green CHECK GLYPH and nothing else — the word is replaced by a mark.
The claimed tile also drops back to the row's base size, giving up the scale-up the claimable tile had, so exactly one tile in the row is ever oversized.
The progress track fills from the left with a solid accent segment covering one seventh of its length, while the '1 / 7 DAYS' text stays centred over the whole track and does not move with the fill.
The footer's right-hand slot swaps content rather than position: 'REWARD READY!' becomes 'NEXT IN 23h 59m 56s'. One slot, two messages, and the countdown only exists when nothing is claimable.
The streak counter at the footer left increments in place ('0 DAY STREAK' to '1 DAY STREAK') — it is a sentence, not a badge.
The red badge on the HUD opener disappears once the claim is taken, and the opener's countdown keeps ticking. The badge tracks claimability, not the existence of the feature.
The session/playtime sibling of the daily screen is a much SMALLER modal — roughly 30% of screen width against the daily panel's 60% — because six gifts need no strip and no streak.
3-across by 2 rows of gifts, and the tile is dropped entirely: the gift artwork IS the tile, with no card, fill or stroke behind it.

rules.note: Distilled from the ten references above. Units are Roblox UI units: px for stroke and radius, screen fractions for panel size, unitless for scale. Proportions were read off screenshots by eye and are stated as approximations. Where the references disagree, the rule says which way the majority goes and what the minority case is for.

layoutByDayCount.upTo7_wideRow: 7 equal tiles in ONE row when the panel is >= 55% of screen width
layoutByDayCount.upTo7_wrapped: 4 across wrapping 4+3, or 3 across wrapping 3+3 with the 7th pulled out, when the panel is narrower or the tiles are square
layoutByDayCount.10plus: a scrolling grid 5 across, with a fixed header and a pinned grand-prize band below the scroll area
layoutByDayCount.emptyCells: leave them empty — never pad the last row with filler tiles
layoutByDayCount.why: all four shipped screens sized the layout to the number of days rather than to a house grid: a 7-day strip runs across in one row, a 7-day set of square tiles wraps 4+3 or 3+3, and the 25-day calendar becomes a 5-wide scroller; a generator that always emits the same column count gets the 25-day case badly wrong

dayTile.aspect: 0.5 (tall portrait) for a one-row strip of 7; 0.9-1.15 (near square) for a wrapped or scrolling grid
dayTile.stroke: none in the default state — the stroke is reserved for the promoted tile
dayTile.why: every reference that draws a tile at all puts the day label on top, the art in the middle and the state at the bottom, in that order and with the state chip against the bottom padding; the aspect is the only thing that changes, and it changes with the layout rather than with the game

stateIsTheChip.rule: state changes the chip at the bottom of the tile; it does not change the reward art
stateIsTheChip.chipWidth: the tile's inner width, edge to edge inside the padding
stateIsTheChip.why: Knockout, the RBLX Essentials kit and the Advent calendar all keep the artwork identical across locked and claimable and move the whole difference into a full-width chip; a chip narrower than the tile reads as a badge and loses the button affordance the player is meant to press

fourStates.claimable: recolour the tile fill to the accent, add a stroke the other tiles do not have, scale the tile up 6-8%, and make the chip a green button reading CLAIM
fourStates.claimed: desaturate the whole tile — fill, art and amount text — and replace the chip's word with a check glyph; drop the tile back to base size
fourStates.locked: leave the art at full colour and full opacity; the chip becomes a neutral or red rect reading LOCKED, or is deleted and replaced by a padlock glyph plus the day number
fourStates.missed: keep the tile, replace the art with a circular-arrow glyph and the chip with RECOVER; grey it when the recovery has been spent
fourStates.why: the claimed frame of the RBLX kit desaturates while the locked tiles beside it stay saturated, and Knockout does the same with a grey Claimed against a red Locked — dimming means SPENT, never NOT YET, and a generator that greys out locked days has told the player their future rewards are already gone

claimableEmphasis.why: three shipped screens change three things at once on the single claimable tile and nothing at all on the others, which is what makes a 7-tile strip readable at a glance; changing only the colour leaves the eye hunting

lockedArt.rule: show the reward at full colour
lockedArt.exception: hide it behind a padlock ONLY when the rewards are meant to be a surprise, as in an advent calendar
lockedArt.why: three of four shipped screens draw locked rewards fully so the player can see what they are waiting for, which is the entire retention argument for the screen; the one that hides them is a calendar whose premise is the unopened door

milestoneDay.footprint: give the final day a different footprint, not just a different colour — a tall card spanning both rows at the end of the grid, or a pinned full-width band below it
milestoneDay.fill: gold or amber with a lighter stroke and an outer glow or sunburst backdrop
milestoneDay.label: replace the numeric quantity with the reward's NAME in one or two lines
milestoneDay.why: Knockout, the RBLX kit and the Advent calendar all promote the last day, and in two of them it stops being a grid cell entirely; the promotion is applied whatever the state says, so fill encodes the prize and the chip still encodes the state

quantity.rule: set the quantity against the art — over its lower corner, or on the line directly beneath it
quantity.never: a bare number, and never its own full row in a square tile
quantity.why: all five tile-drawing references prefix the number and place it against the art; giving it its own row is what forces the tile tall, and a square tile has no room for it

countdownFormat.underADay: Xh Ym Zs when it is the panel's single headline timer, Xh Ym when it is one of many
countdownFormat.units: two, three only for the headline timer
countdownFormat.suffixes: unit letters (d/h/m/s); the pure clock form HH:MM:SS is the minority variant
countdownFormat.never: a bare seconds count, and never a unit that is showing zero
countdownFormat.why: five independent screens were read and all of them drop the coarsest unit once it hits zero and carry at most three; the letter-suffix form appears in four of five, the colon form in one, so the suffix form is the default and the clock form is a choice

countdownPlacement.nextClaimTimer: one instance only, in the header beside the title, directly under the header, or in the footer's right-hand slot
countdownPlacement.perTileTimer: only when each entry unlocks on its own clock, and then it goes inside that tile's state chip
countdownPlacement.overArt: a timer may sit centred on the artwork only when the tile has no state chip
countdownPlacement.mutualExclusion: the next-claim timer and the READY message occupy the SAME slot and never both appear
countdownPlacement.why: the RBLX kit swaps 'REWARD READY!' for 'NEXT IN 23h 59m 56s' in one footer slot, which is the whole logic of the screen: a countdown exists precisely when nothing is claimable, and showing both at once tells the player two contradictory things

streakCounter.rule: a footer-anchored label and number — 'N DAY STREAK' or 'STREAK: N' — with the number heavier or brighter than the word
streakCounter.position: a bottom corner, opposite the status slot
streakCounter.never: leaving the streak implied by which tile is highlighted
streakCounter.why: the strip repeats every 5 or 7 days while the streak does not, and Adopt Me shows 'STREAK: 110' against a five-tile cycle precisely so the repetition does not read as lost progress; a screen with no counter silently resets the player's sense of investment every week

progressTrack.shape: a full-width pill with an outline, spanning the strip, directly under it
progressTrack.textInsideTheTrack: 'N / 7 DAYS' centred over the whole track, not moving with the fill
progressTrack.fill: a solid accent segment from the left, one cell's width per claimed day
progressTrack.alternative: for a gift set with no day order, a plain line reading 'N/M Rewards claimed' instead of a bar
progressTrack.why: the RBLX kit centres the fraction over the track so it stays legible at 1/7 and at 6/7, whereas a label that rides the fill is unreadable at both ends; the gift panel drops the bar entirely because six unordered gifts have no progress to draw

claimAction.oneClaimableAtATime: the claim button lives ON the claimable tile, as its state chip
claimAction.manyClaimableAtOnce: one primary button in the footer that claims everything ready, and the tiles carry read-only READY chips
claimAction.loginPopup: no claim button at all — an auto-shown popup grants the reward by appearing, and its only control is close
claimAction.why: Roblox's own package uses a single footer 'Claim Rewards' button because several Time rewards can be Ready together, while every day-strip screen puts CLAIM on the one tile — the rule follows from how many things can be claimed, not from taste

header.style: an inset band across the panel's top inner edge is the majority; an overhanging plaque or free-standing title is the minority
header.titleAlign: left in a band, centred when the title is free-standing
header.carries: the countdown or the tab row, to the side of the title
header.why: the two kits and the calendar all use a full-width inset band while the two shipped games overhang the title, so unlike the simulator genre the rewards screen does NOT demand a plaque; what is constant is that the header band carries a second thing beside the title

closeButton.position: top-right, in or above the header band
closeButton.why: the rewards screen is the one screen that varies here — a bare glyph on Roblox's package, a rounded square on Adopt Me, a proud red mark on Knockout — so the rule is position, not shape, and a generator should take the shape from the theme rather than hard-coding a circle

panelSize.dayStrip: 55-65% of screen width, 35-45% of screen height
panelSize.why: measured by eye across four shipped panels; a six-gift panel drawn at day-strip width is mostly empty, and a 7-tile strip drawn at gift-panel width forces the tiles to wrap for no reason

hudOpener.rule: the screen always has a persistent on-screen opener of its own, pinned to a screen edge
hudOpener.carries: a live countdown directly beneath the icon, and a red badge dot when something is claimable
hudOpener.badgeTracksClaimability: the badge appears and disappears with the claim, not with the feature
hudOpener.why: Roblox's package ships a named RewardsHudButton and the RBLX kit pins a countdown-bearing icon stack to the left edge; without an opener that badges itself the player only discovers a waiting reward by opening a menu on a hunch

autoOpen.rule: open the screen on join when a reward is claimable, and never when one is not
autoOpen.why: Roblox's own package defaults isHiddenOnJoin to false and describes the pop-up as conditional on a new claimable daily reward; a screen that opens on every join becomes a thing the player dismisses without reading

options: a fixed daily reset time shared by all players
resetPolicy.storedAs: a timestamp the countdown counts toward, not a day counter
resetPolicy.documentedEdge: under a fixed-reset policy a player who claims at 23:00 can claim again at 00:00, one hour later
resetPolicy.why: Roblox's docs spell out both policies and that exact edge case; a generator that counts days rather than storing the next claimable timestamp cannot render a countdown at all, which is the screen's most-looked-at element

rarityLayer.rule: rarity is a swapped background frame behind the tile contents, chosen by the reward's own effect field, never a tint applied to the state chip
rarityLayer.why: Roblox's package implements valuable rewards as a different frame added to RewardItemFrames, and Knockout's amber spin-day tile still carries an ordinary Locked button — keeping the two in separate layers is what stops a rare locked reward from looking claimable

missedDayRecovery.rule: keep the missed tile in place; replace its art with a recover glyph and its chip with RECOVER, and grey the chip once the recovery is spent
missedDayRecovery.why: the Advent calendar keeps missed days visible and sellable rather than deleting them, and the kit's own listing describes missing a day as pausing the cycle rather than resetting it — a strip that removes missed days loses the row's arithmetic and the offer

themeTheFrameNotTheGrid.rule: spend the game's theme on the panel chrome — an ice frame, a notepad spiral, a festive hat over the header — and keep the tiles inside strictly rectangular and systematic
themeTheFrameNotTheGrid.why: both shipped games wrap an illustrated frame around a grid that stays plain, which is what lets seven tiles read as one comparable set; theming the tiles themselves is what turns a reward strip into decoration the eye cannot scan

screens.label: Settings / Options screen (toggle rows, sliders, sectioned groups, keybind rows, close & reset affordances)
demonstrates: the settings panel is a CENTRED LANDSCAPE modal, not a tall sheet: AnchorPoint 0.5, Position (0.5,0,0.5,0), Size (0.75,0,0.75,0) with a UIAspectRatioConstraint of 2.5 — two and a half times wider than tall
its pixel width is CLAMPED, not free: UISizeConstraint MinSize (350,0), MaxSize (800,inf) — so the panel stops growing on a monitor and stops shrinking on a phone
UICorner is given in SCALE (0.1,0), so the radius tracks the panel's own height instead of being a fixed pixel value

close is an ImageButton with AnchorPoint (1,0) at Position (1,-10,0,10) — pinned to the panel's top-right with a 10px inset — sized (0.15,0,0.15,0) and forced square by a UIAspectRatioConstraint; it is an icon, not a labelled button

a slider ROW is a transparent container at Size (0.8,0,0.1,0) — 80% of the panel wide, 10% of it tall — laid out by a UIListLayout with FillDirection Horizontal, HorizontalFlex Fill, VerticalAlignment Center and Padding (0.06,0)
the row's leading icon is an ImageLabel at Size (2.5,0,2.5,0) with a 1:1 UIAspectRatioConstraint — 250% of the row height, so the icon deliberately overflows the row's vertical band
the slider TRACK is a fully round bar: UICorner (0.5,0), UIStroke Thickness 3, and a UISizeConstraint MaxSize (inf,30) that caps its height at 30px however tall the panel gets

the FILL is a separate frame anchored (0,0.5) at Position (0,0,0.5,0), Size (0.5,0,1,0), ZIndex 2, UICorner (0.5,0) — it grows rightward from the track's left edge and is the accent colour at BackgroundTransparency 0.35

the KNOB is a circle at Size (1.2,0,1.2,0) — 120% of the track, so it OVERHANGS the track top and bottom — with a 1:1 aspect constraint, UICorner (0.5,0), a UIStroke of Thickness 8 in the accent colour, and ZIndex 3 so it sits over the fill
the accent colour appears on the fill and on the knob's stroke; the track itself stays neutral (black at BackgroundTransparency 0.75)
dragging is a UIDragDetector with DragStyle TranslateLine, ResponseStyle Scale and BoundingUI set to the track — the knob cannot leave the bar, and the value is read in scale, not pixels

open/close is asymmetric motion: open tweens Position from (0.5,0.4) to (0.5,0.5) with bounce easing over 0.5s and sets Visible true; close sets Visible false with a 0-second duration — the panel rises with an overshoot and vanishes instantly

the settings surface is a TAB inside a menu ('Settings', alongside Report, Help, Record), opened with Esc and closed with an X in the corner or a Resume button — the wiki notes the X and the Resume button have co-existed across menu versions

row control types are a closed set: an on/off toggle (Shift Lock, Full screen), a named-option selector (Camera mode cycles Follow / Classic / CameraToggle / Default; Movement mode cycles Keyboard / Keyboard + Mouse / Click to Move; Graphics mode is Manual / Automatic), and a DISCRETE BAR slider
the discrete slider is counted in bars, not percent: mouse sensitivity and volume are 'one bar being the slowest, and ten bars being the fastest', and volume has a real zero — 'No bars being mute'
a row the developer has disabled is GREYED OUT and left in place, not removed: 'This option would be greyed out if the owner disabled changing camera modes' — same for movement mode
a DEPENDENT row stays visible and becomes adjustable only when its parent row allows it: graphics quality is adjustable 'as long as the graphics mode is set to manual'
typed numeric entry was removed from the sensitivity row in May 2020 — decimals like 0.25 revert to 0 on Enter, so the bar count is the only input

in 2022 the Controls list was MOVED OUT of Help and INTO the settings surface, and version readouts (Client / Server / Place / CoreScript version) were put behind an 'Advanced Settings' category at the bottom
the header is ONE ROW, name left and close right: a flex row with justify-content space-between, the word 'Settings' at font-size 300%, and a close-button image at the right at 45x45px

the panel in the recreation is 500px wide, border 2px solid, border-radius 8px, padding 4px 20px — a narrow radius and a thin border, i.e. the settings panel does NOT inherit the fat cartoon stroke a simulator shop panel gets
rows are grouped under ALL-CAPS section headers with no box around them — here 'VOLUME' then 'MISC' — and the rows hang directly beneath

the row markup names the control type per row, and only two types appear: 'adjust bar' (Lobby Music, Game Music) and 'toggle' carrying its default state ('toggle on' for Toggle Crouch, 'toggle off' for Reduce Motion and Hide Own Clothes)
volume is split into TWO rows by context — Lobby Music and Game Music — rather than one master volume
a row can be platform-exclusive: Toggle Crouch is described as 'a PC and Console exclusive setting'

the settings a horror game ships are reduce-effects rows, not graphics rows: Reduce Motion ('disables or enables the camera tilt when turning... for people who may experience dizziness') and Hide Own Clothes (stated as a performance/visibility setting present 'in many more Roblox games')
the entry point is a GEAR ICON in the top HUD, reachable 'on any Device (PC, Mobile, Controller) from the Top HUD Gear Icon both in-match and in the lobby' — the same screen serves menu and match
the page states the contract outright: 'Some Options May Vary By Device'
sections are named by domain, not by control type: Audio Options, Game Options, Friends, Privacy, Controls (PC Only) — and a section may hold a single row (Friends holds only Friend Notifications)
three separate volume sliders, one per sound group: Emote Music Volume, Game Background Music Volume, Lobby Background Music Volume
a numeric range row states its bounds and its default in the UI's own terms: FOV 'is set to 80 as default. (70 - 100)'
rows are HIDDEN, not greyed, when the platform can never use them: 'Mobile Shift Lock (Mobile Only)... It is not visible on PC', and 'PC Shift Lock (PC Only)'
the whole Controls section is PC-only, and it carries a scoped reset: the listed controls 'can be Changed in the Settings Menu' and 'can also be Reset To Default'
a setting can also be a hotkey: Picture Mode 'can Also Be Turned on/off Using [F1] on PC' — so a toggle row and a keybind can name the same state
role-gated rows exist and are simply absent for everyone else: Enable Freecam 'is Only Available for Developers, Anti-Cheat Moderators, Famous Role and Roblox Star Creator'
defaults are stated per row throughout ('Turned On By Default', 'Turned Off by Default'), i.e. the screen is expected to know its own defaults
when the groups pass three, they become TABS: 'The Settings Menu has 4 categories, Video, Audio, Gameplay and Controls' — each category is its own page of rows with its own screenshot
group sizes are small: Video 3 rows, Audio 5, Gameplay 6, Controls 5 — nothing approaching a twenty-row flat list
sliders are stated in normalised units with the display caveat spelled out: Master / Soundtrack / Environment Volume each default to 1, 'however, that 1 here actually means 100%'

a numeric row is not a slider: Snap to Grid Range, Rotate Amount, 'Shift' Rotate Amount and 'Ctrl' Rotate Amount are typed values with stated ranges (rotation 1-360 degrees, defaults 45 / 90 / 15) and are COMMITTED by a separate control — 'Setting this to a value and clicking the check'
